speechtext:
That an humble address be presented to His Most Excellent Majesty the King, in the following words: We, Your Majesty's most dutiful and loyal subjects, the (	) House of Commons of Canada,
in parliament assembled, humbly approach Your Majesty, praying that you may graciously be pleased to give your consent to submit a measure to the Parliament of the United Kingdom to amend the British North America Act, 1867, in the manner following, or to the following effect:-
Total payment

B. N. A. Act Amendment
" An Act to amend the British North America Act. 1867.
"Be it enacted by the King's Most Excellent Majesty, by and with the advice and consent of the Lords, Spiritual and Temporal, and the Commons, in this present parliament assembled, and by the authority of same as follows:
" 1. This Act may be cited as the British North America Act, 1925.
" 2. The parliament of the Dominion may amend the said British North America Act when it may see fit to do so, but it is not empowered to pass any amendment affecting the rights guaranteed in said act to minorities.
" 3. The proposed law for the alteration of the said act must be passed by an absolute majority of each house of parliament."
All of which we humbly pray Your Majesty to take into your favourable and gracious consideration.
He said:	Mr. Speaker, in the debate on
the Address I took occasion to deal with a matter in which I think Canada has a vital interest, concerning, as it does, the constitution of this country and the rights of the people and parliament. My reason for directing the attention of the House to the subject was the judgment which had been delivered a few days previously by the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council in England, in connection with the Industrial Disputes Investigation Act. The constitutionality of that act was questioned before that committee and the act was declared1 by the committee to be ultra vires of the powers of the Dominion parliament. That seemed to me an invasion of what I regard as the rights of Canada; or, if it was not an invasion of those rights, it was at least of such a character as to make us realize that the time has arrived when we in this parliament should go into the question of our constitution and the question of our rights and determine whether we should longer remain subject to the decision of a court in the creation of which we had no voice.
The Judicial Committee of the Privy Council is a body of the highest legal standing. We all respect it; we have no objection to its findings; I believe its finding in this case was right in law. But to my mind such decisions are not in the interests of the development of this country in a constitutional way. I am confident that this parliament has only to ask that some kind of relief be afforded and the request will be granted, thus placing the interpretation of the constitution of Canada within our own country rather than outside of it.
Now, the only constitution we have for Canada is the document which I hold in my hand, the British North America Act. This copy is the official copy printed by parliament -I got it from the Senate-of "The British North America Acts, 1867-1907," and I contend that any change in or improvement of the constitution of Canada must be by way
iMr. W. P. Maclean.]
of amendment to these acts, and that the place to make those amendments is in this parliament. I go further and say that it is the duty of this parliament to cause that constitution to be amended so that the same rights may be conceded to us as have been granted by the Imperial parliament to Australia, in large measure to South Africa, and finally to Ireland. If you examine these constitutions which have been created since the passing of these British North America Acts you will find that they widen as they go down. I was surprised to find upon investigation that in the case of the Irish Free State, the last one created, the constitution is wider than any of the others and there is the least interference. A little later I will deal with that matter more specifically and perhaps throw a little light upon it.
I am not a lawyer; I am only a lay member of this House, but I have watched the proceedings of the House and the sentiment of the people throughout the country and I can see that there is a growing feeling in the minds of the people that the time has come when we ought to have what Australia has, what South Africa has, what the Free State of south Ireland has-the right to make our owp constitution; to amend it and to have it interpreted in our own courts. We shall then be in a position in this parliament and in the provincial parliaments to adjust the law so as to suit the interpretation made by our own courts.

cases of federations, except Ireland, and we know something about federations in this country; we have had experience with a federation. Our great neighbour to the south of us, the United States, is also a federation, and my contention is that the construction of such constitutions can be accomplished better in the country that is a federation than in the Mother Country. I have approached the question in my amendment in the fairest possible way. I have observed the regular method of procedure. The amendment has respect in every word of it for His Majesty the King and for the Imperial parliament, and most of all it conserves and protects the rights of minorities guaranteed by our constitution. So I think it is a very reasonable amendment. What I propose is:

"Be it enacted by the King's Most Excellent Majesty, by and with the advice and consent of the Lords, Spiritual and Temporal, and the Commons, in this present parliament assembled, and by the authority of same as follows:
" 1. This act may be cited as the British North America Act, 1925.
" 2. The parliament of the Dominion may amend the said British North America Act when it may see fit to do so, but it is not empowered to pass any amendment affecting the rights guaranteed in said act to minorities.

subtopic: PROPOSED CHANGE IN METHOD OF MAKING
speechtext: What does the Iron, member mean by an absolute majority?

subtopic: PROPOSED CHANGE IN METHOD OF MAKING
speechtext:
I will come to
that in a moment. I have put that in a very simple way. I maintain that no one is so competent to deal with the federation as we Canadians are, and as the other countries are that are united in a system of federation. While I have every respect for the Old Country and for the judges of the Old Country, they have not quite the experience that we have of the system of federation for the government of a country. It is true they have had a good deal to do with federations since they have been established here and in the other dominions, but they have not got to deal with these questions that are vital to us and that are coming up every day. There is a dispute now between the federal and provincial powers in this country, as there is in Australia, and the same is the case in the United States. The result in the United
States is that they have created one of the greatest courts in the world for the interpretation of federation law. Theirs is a federation; so is ours, so is Australia's so is South Africa's, and so will be others, for others are to come. As I said, the United States has had wide experience. We are getting wide experience, and the British parliament has not had that experience with federations so far that would qualify it to be the final interpreter of their constitutions. The British parliament is concerned with the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland. It is concerned with one great island, England, Scotland and Wales, and with a small portion of the north of Ireland. That great island is governed by a parliament which has absolute power. There is no parliament in the world that has the absolute, full and free power that the parliament of Great Britain has. As I pointed out to this House the other day, they can by a single act change the succession to the crown, repeal Magna Charta, and disestablish the English Church; they can do all that by one single act of parliament. We have a different arrangement here. We are not as free as they are. We are more or less governed by this system of federation. We have a federation and we cannot get away from it, and so we must have a constitution applying to a federation. We must have it interpreted in Canada, and I believe that our Supreme court is fitted to become the final authority to decide cases in dispute as between the federal and provincial powers.
Just to show what the difference is between the two systems, and what has taken place, what concessions have been made to the other dominions, I am going to read from the latest deliverance that has been made on this, matter. I have here The Constitution, Administration and Laws of the Empire by A. Berriedale Keith, D.C.L., of the Inner Temple, barrister-at-law, and of the Scottish bar, Regius Professor of Sanskrit and Comparative Philology at the university of Edinburgh, formerly of the Colonial Office, author of Responsible Government in the Dominions, and so forth. Professor Keith is the latest authority on this question, and his book, which I now have in my hand, is dated one year ago to-day less two days. This book was published in London just about one year ago to-day, and it is the latest deliverance on the subject. I am going to read a short extract which helps a lot to clear the situation. On page 22 of this book, in dealing with colonial legislatures, he says:

B. N. A. Act Amendment
The existing restrictions on constitutional change differ greatly in various parts of the Empire. In Canada the provinces enjoy freedom in great measure, but only within the limited sphere of their own powers under the British North America Act; they cannot alter the division of powers between them and the Dominion, nor can they affect the office of Lieutenant-Governor as the executive link between them and the Dominion. The Dominion, on the other hand, has extremely limited powers, because the federation was a compact between the provinces, and it is held to be illegitimate for the federal parliament to change the terms of that compact, unless with general assent from the provinces. Imperial acts were therefore necessary in 1907 to alter the amounts of the provincial subsidies, in 1915 to readjust the representation of the provinces in the Senate, and in 1916 to extend the duration of parliament by a year. The desire of the Dominion to obtain wider constituent powers is natural but no agreement on the subject exists with the provinces, as Quebec fears that any change might lessen the security for the equal treatment of the French language in federal proceedings, and the position of the Roman Catholic Church.
Next he deals with Australia:
The Commonwealth of Australia has the widest constituent powers, to be exercised by absolute majorities in both houses of parliament, approved by a referendum of the electors-
There is where the leader of the Progressive party gets his answer. There must be an absolute majority of both the houses in Australia to effect the changes in the constitution.

speechtext:
Is not that provided for
in the Australian constitution?

subtopic: PROPOSED CHANGE IN METHOD OF MAKING
speechtext:
Yes, I know, but let me finish the quotation:
-but one house may secure at the discretion of the Governor General a referendum by passing a bill for a change twice, an interval of three months intervening. There arises, however, the question whether any change abandoning the federal character of the constitution is possible; the answer would seem to be in the negative. The States have full powers of constitutional change, but within the limits of the federal constitution; bills effecting important alterations or dealing with the governor's salary must be reserved unless approved in advance by the Imperial government. Efforts to effect by referendum great changes in the relation of the states and the Commonwealth have so far been defeated at the polls, and the question of a revision of the constitution which would probably involve Imperial legislation, is still unsolved.
Now I come to New Zealand, and I have got very little more to read:
New Zealand originally had somewhat limited powers of constitutional change, but it is probable that since the act of 1865 she has practically full authority in this regard, though any important constitutional change would probably be effected by a bill reserved for the signification of the royal assent. The same position applies to Newfoundland where the constitution rests on the prerogative. In the Union of South Africa changes affecting the numbers and distribution of seats in the lower house, the native franchise in the Cape province, and the equality of the Dutch and English languages can be brought about only by a two-thirds majority of both houses at a joint sitting, and the same rule applies to any proposal to vary this requirement. Moreover, any bill affecting the constitution

or powers of the provincial councils, or the provisions regarding the lower house must be reserved. In Malta power of alteration, by two-thirds majorities of the total members of either house, is limited to matters not affecting the subjects of legislative power, religious toleration, the rules regarding official languages, and the civil list, and in the case of India under the provisional constitution power of change in any essentials is reserved to parliament.
India is altogether different from Canada I hope. Now I eome to legislation in the crown colonies:
The legislatures in the crown colonies and protectorates have as a rule no constituent powers, but those of the colonies with representative legislatures have full legal powers of alteration. In the Irish Free State the power of alteration is limited only by the necessity of not violating the treaty of December 6, 1921, and by the requirement that after eight years from December 6, 1922, changes must be approved by referendum.
There is a short and succinct history of the way in which the constitutions are provided with their amendments in the various acts which have passed the British parliament. Canada, which was the first to be created, is limited ever so much more than the other later dominions, and yet we by reason of our fifty-seven years of experience, by reason of our contribution in the war-of men, of money and other things-are at least entitled to the same equality of privilege in the matter of amending our constitution as these other states enjoy. And that is not all. We entered upon this undertaking long before many of the other dominions. Long ago we achieved responsible government in this country, but it was obtained by a battle, and we have been recognized as an equal state by certain declarations that have been made in England. We have been given a position on the League of Nations, and we have been recognized in other directions. The Parliament of Canada has achieved another thing. Canada has achieved the right to negotiate a treaty and to sign it through a Canadian minister and we are making headway in various other ways. You can go through the correspondence which has taken place between the Mother Country and Canada, and you see a gradual widening out not so much in the direction of independence as in the recognition of the fact that the more freedom is given to Canada the stronger she will be in domestic affairs and the broader and stronger will be the union between the daughter state and the Mother Country. That is my contention. I am asking only that Canada be given what these other countries possess, and we can get it in a moment; all we have to do is ask for it. Some of my friends will say "Why should we ask for it?" Because the sentiment is growing, and England sees more and more that the way to be

B. N. A. Act Amendment
strong in the estimation of the dominions, including Canada, is to give them every freedom in the management of their own affairs. This right will be given to us if we ask for it. For the present condition of affairs I blame our own parliament and our own governments past and present. They are to be blamed because they 'have not asked for this right. I am just as certain as that I am standing here that we have only to ask in the way I have indicated and the right will be conceded. Was any objection made when Canada asserted the right to sign her own treaty? No, there was no objection there, it was rather welcomed and, as I have said, this parliament is to blame because we have not been given full power to make our own constitution.
Now I have come to my real argument and it is this: Is Canada a sovereign state? Are we a nation? If we have not the right to make our own constitution and to make our own courts the final interpreter of it, ought we not to have the right when a legal decision is needed to have it made here in Canada by a court which is the creation of this Dominion? Canada creates her own courts, and why should she not be given the jurisdiction to settle these constitutional questions? I think the time has arrived when she should have this right, and I think the people of this country are of the same opinion. Some persons have said to me, "Oh Mr. Maclean, when you spoke in the House the other day you talked of the judicial committee having shot holes in the constitution of Canada. Are you not shooting holes in the British constitutionI say no. The whole history of British connection is one of the development of progressive government, of the increase of the liberties of the people concerned, and it must be admitted that in that way greater union is secured. Now, I am not the only offender in this matter. The right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen) has a very strong notice of motion on the order paper in regard to Canada's independence in the matter of fiscal and tariff policy. I know that I am going to have the support of the right hon. gentleman in this matter because I am only trying to do in regard to it what he is trying to do with respect to our fiscal policy He is following the late Sir John A. Macdonald. John A. achieved a good deal. He is responsible for the National Policy in this country; and if we achieved a national policy in regard to the tariff God knows it is time to achieve it in regard to the constitution of the country so as to render our courts supreme in matters of law.
I could go on and speak at length on this question but I do not intend to do so. This
is a short sitting and I should like to see some definite pronouncement made from authoritative quarters. But, I hope the House will adopt this proposal. There may be an objection to it, and I am waiting to hear that objection. I am especially waiting to hear from the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) and from the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) as to whether they are prepared to ask for relief in this matter. I do noit wish to sidestep the issue, and I am not prepared to say whether there ought to be a consultation between the provinces and the Dominion, although that is set out in Professor Keith's book; but the point is that if we unite on this matter we will get relief. All you have to do is to ask the British government to-day to adopt what I have in substance embodied in my resolution. It is a simple proposal and will not be denied. I believe that if we pass the resolution this session we will obtain relief 'before the end of the year and then Canada will be in a position to undertake what is her right to undertake, which is the natural outcome of our progress; to make her own constitution, and to interpret it in her own country via the 'Supreme court, which is composed of responsible Canadians.
I have not a word to say in regard to the constitution of the Privy Council. People say it is a good thing that we can go there, and I give the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council credit for having time after time saved the country in the interpretation of the constitution from mistakes of her own parliament and legislature, but we are not always to be in the position of minors. After 57 years of experience under the British North America Act the statement is made, "Oh you are minors, you are colonials." Have we not advanced beyond the state of being minors or mere colonials? Has that state of affairs not ceased? Or when is it to cease? Are we not of age? In the old days we relied on the fathers of the constitution. They are all gone. We must take care of ourselves and work out our own salvation and our own autonomy exactly on the lines I have suggested to-day; but the matter has to be dealt with and considered in some way. I hope that never again will we be in the position that the interpretation of the British North America Act must be made by the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council. I think now is the time to end that state of affairs, and I say that with all respect to the judicial committee and to the Mother Country. It has given greater rights to the other dominions. They are prepared to give the same rights to the Canadian people, and especially to these Canadian people who
2S8

B. N. A. Act Amendment
have the record that we have as a free state and as a great ally of the Mother Country. They are prepared to give it to us if we ask for it. Objections of one kind and another can be raised, and they are worthy of consideration, but the broad question i3 now up before this House and the other chamber.
I am appealing most of all to the right hon. leader of the opposition in regard to these matters, and perhaps he will be ab'e to let the members of another honourable House see that they should join the House in the proposal as I have set it out; and if he does so it will be easy to get ahead and make some improvement. I absolutely dissent from the statement that has been made in this House, in the country and in another place, that in some way Canada is still in a state of tutelage, and that we are minors and that we have the right to go to the foot of the throne as the Indian has the right. We are not Indians. We are full-blooded Canadians, and a hundred per cent Canadians, as I said the other day, and if this Canadian parliament in this year 1925 is not fit to make its own constitution, and if its courts are not fit to interpret that constitution, when will we be in such a position? Does the leader of the House, a Canadian, hold that view? Does the Minister of Justice hold that view? Are his colleagues of that view? Are hon. gentlemen on this side of the House and are our friends from the west of that view?
I should like to talk about some reports that have been mentioned in the press in regard to constitutional changes in this country, but I respect the question that I have submitted to the House too much to deal with these reports in any way. I may have occasion at the close of this debate to say a few words on the objections that may be urged* against my proposition, and when I speak about objections being urged against it I wish to say to my fellow countrymen that I am a Canadian and I have tried to protect all rights as set out in the original act. I have not made a single suggestion to repeal in any way anything which is calculated to protect the rights of the minority under this act. I think I wall have support in this matter, because a lot of other questions will come up. The constitution must be broadened. New aLlianees and new formations will take place, and I repeat that the only way to settle the constitution is to make this act the basis of it. You cannot go outside and create new acts, but it must all be embodied in this one act. You can expand it, and in expanding it you must protect the rights within that constitution. It must follow, as 
daylight follows darkness, and foe based on this act. The whole question before us now is this act and how we can amend it so as to make self-government more complete in Canada, and therefore make this a better country in which to live, and to work out the destiny which is in store for us. There may be still a great federation for us in the future in connection with the British Empire. I am not going into that. That would be based on federal ideas. But as we are now a federated nation and have federal laws and are living under those laws, nobody is so competent to deal with this question as ourselves. That being so I leave the motion with the House.

B. Ar. A. Act Amendment
Mr. MARTEiLL:	The trend, however, of
my hon. friend's remarks has been an endeavour to show that we should not in any wise appeal to the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council in matters of law in the Dominion of Canada. It will be well for us for a few minutes to consider how confederation was brought about and what is the present charter of the Dominion of Canada. It is a matter of common history that negotiations took place from time to time between what was then commonly called Canada, that is, Ontario and Quebec, and the provinces of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick, looking to the consummation of a federal union. As a result of the Quebec conference, I think in October, 1864, certain resolutions were passed, and in accordance with these resolutions there was passed by the Imperial parliament an enactment known as the British North America Act. The British North America Act of 1867, under which Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Quebec and Ontario were federally united, is the charter or constitution of the Dominion of Canada. It is in the nature of a contract between the various provinces. The minds of the fathers of confederation, as we say in the law of contracts, eventually got ad idem, that is to say, they came to a common meeting point. Confederation did not alter in any respect our relationship towards Great Britain or weaken in any way the headship of the crown. There is in the British North America Act nothing which in any way vacates the supreme legislative authority of the British parliament over and throughout the British Empire. To say that our position as one of the nations within the British Empire is on an equality with that of the British parliament as regards legislative authority is to assert an anachronism. The British parliament can change the imperial constitution; it can also change the constitution of any of the daughter nations within the empire, whereas Canada cannot alter her own constitution nor in any wise affect the constitution of Great Britain. No legislative body can make laws repugnant to imperial acts, which by express words or necessary intendment are extended to the British dominions beyond the seas.
My hon. friend, moreover, has said that we are a nation, a sovereign nation. Every person who knows the primary essentials of international law must know that no nation is a sovereign nation unless it has the right to send and receive ambassadors, a right which Canada has not at the 4 p.m. present time. There are several acts which have been expressly applied to Canada, the chief of these being 19
the British North America Act, which is our Canadian charter or constitution. The resolution of the hon. member for South York, which embraces within its four quarters a draft petition to His Most Gracious Majesty the King, praying that Canada be given the right to amend her own constitution, is in itself a violation of the contract made between Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Quebec and Ontario at the time of confederation. This contract became law by the ratification of the Imperial parliament, and the contract is the British North America Act. It will be remembered that at the Quebec conference, held for the purpose of bringing about a confederation of the provinces of Canada, Nova Scotia and New Brunswick, resolutions were passed which became the basis of what is known as the British North America Act. Prior to confederation each of the provinces of Canada was as plenary in its power of government and legislation as is the Dominion of Canada to-day and also the various legislatures; that is to say, the various provinces which now constitute Canada, particularly the provinces of Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Quebec and Ontario, at the time of confederation possessed all the powers of civil government embraced in the powers and authority of both the federal parliament and the provincial legislatures combined at the present time. The British North America Act may be termed the contract between the provinces and the federal authority.
To attempt in any wise to interfere with the British North America Act, which as I say, was an agreement between the various provinces of Canada, ratified and confirmed by the British parliament, without conference and agreement between the provinces constituting confederation and the federal authorities, would be a wrongful act. It would be a violation of the crassest kind of provincial rights, and without the concurrence of the various provinces constituting confederation, a petition based upon a resolution such as has been moved by my hon. friend would not be entertained by His Most Gracious Majesty in Council or by the Imperial parliament. Where there has been entered into between two parties a contract, the making of which has been the subject of a great deal of negotiation, it cannot be altered so as to give one of the parties rights and privileges without the concurrence ad idem of the other parties to the pact. In ordinary contracts between individual and individual, if a contract is reduced to writing, then one of the parties cannot of his own volition insert a new covenant without being guilty of a breach of contract. In a greater

B. N. A. Act Amendment

question where the rights of minorities, the rights of provincial legislatures are concerned, my hon. friend is endeavouring to have a unilateral change, so to speak, of the constitution or charter of Canada made between the parties at the time the confederation of Canada was brought about. At that time the various provinces which went into confederation surrendered rights to a central body, but they retained certain rights to themselves. The agreement or contract was the British North America Act, and surely no person would hold that one of the parties to that agreement has the right to alter it without the consent of all the parties interested. In an ordinary civil matter, to do so would be a breach of the agreement; then if this is so as between individual and individual, how much greater is the wrong when it affects the constitutional rights of sections of provinces of the Dominion of Canada?
The jurisdiction of the Canadian parliament to alter the Canadian constitution cannot be conceded and have the rights of the provinces protected. The will of the Canadian parliament in this matter is not omnipotent; the superior authority is the Imperial parliament. The question to be decided as regards any Canadian legislation, whether federal or provincial, is simply this: Is the act repugnant to the British North America Act? Does the act overstep the limits prescribed by the Imperial charter for federal or provincial legislation, as the case may be? A statute emanating from a legislature not having the power to pass it is not law. A legislative body cannot confer rights or impose liabilities where the legislature has no power to pass such a law. It is a nullitas nullitatum and cannot affect anybody. The British North America Act which has prescribed the bounds of the legislative authority of both federal and provincial legislatures imposes upon the judges of our courts the duty of seeing that those bounds are not over-ruled.
Now, Sir, I have dealt with the question of contract; let me come to the question of appeal to the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council. That seems to be the chief theme of my hon. friend's discussion. It has been brought about by the declaration of the judicial committee that the Industrial Disputes Act of 1907 is ultra vires of the federal parliament. I am not going to criticise that act. Its object was commendable. But no matter how commendable the object, no matter what may be the desire of the people in any part of this country, it does not give to parliament the right to infringe upon the rights of other parties to the contract. I might
'Mr Martall.]
review the reasons why the decision was given. It was the subject of a dispute in the city of Toronto between the Hydro Electric Commission and its employees. A board of conciliation was appointed by the Minister of Labour of the day. The Hydro Electric Commission said that this was not in the best interests of the parties to the dispute, and they refused to appoint their representative. Under the act it is provided that once a board is appointed all things remain in statu quo. The Hydro Electric Commission contended that by virtue of clause 13 of section 92 of the British North America Act the provincial legislature was the only legislative authority capable of passing such legislation. Application was made to Mr. Justice Orde in chambers, and after hearing argument His Lordship granted a restraining order pending the trial. Mr. Justice Mowat tried the case, and he upheld the validity of the act, Appeal from his judgment was taken to the appellate court of Ontario, which upheld the trial judge, Mr. Justice Hodgins dissenting. The matter was then taken to the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council, and their Lordships decided that the act was an infringement upon clause 13 of section 92 of the British North America Act, and was therefore ultra vires of the federal parliament to enact.
In the course of his disquisition my hon. friend said that the Privy Council was right in its decision. That in itself, Mr. Speaker, is one of the strongest arguments why the right of appeal to the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council should be maintained. There is no clamour throughout the length and breadth of the Dominion for the abolition of such appeals. The Judicial Committee of the Privy Council is made up of some of the highest trained lawyers in the British Empire, men who have devoted themselves exclusively to the study and practice of law. The great barristers of England who are elevated to the bench are not men, as we often find in some of our courts, closely allied to corporations- business men rather than lawyers. The judges of England have been trained from their youth in the principles of Blackstone, of Coke and of Littleton. And it is an ideal state of affairs that we, whose forbears brought with them all the common law of England save that which was inapplicable to our status as a colony, should have these principles of common law made uniform in interpretation for the whole British Empire.
The Judicial Committee of the Privy Council as at present constituted-and, Mr. Speaker, I take this from a speech made by one of the law lords in the House of Lords

B. N. -4. Act Amendment
many years ago-took its origin in 1833, and it is the general concurrence of opinion that that tribunal has performed its very high and important functions,-a great if not the principal portion of which has been the exercise of appellate jurisdiction in cases brought from the various portions of the British Empire-to the satisfaction both of Great Britain and her dominions beyond the seas. I submit that from the date when that learned law lord made that statement down to the present time there is not a single person in the Dominion who, if he is fair, wants in any way to interfere with the right of appeal to the Privy Council. We are satisfied with it, and we should devote ourselves to domestic problems, leaving the law as it is in that regard.
It should be the primary condition of all legislation throughout the British Empire to have the law not repugnant to the law of England. We have ample precedents for interpretation. It is easy to find a decision when we go to the English courts, because there has been the long trend of ages wherein interpretations have been made by the greatest lawyers of England. I say, Sir, it should be the primary condition of all legislation throughout the British Empire to have the law not repugnant to the law of England, save in so far as changes by statute are necessary from time to time in order to meet conditions obtaining in particular sections of one of the constituent parts of the empire. It is accepted that the first settlers brought to Canada. were bound by all the principles of the common law of England which were applicable to our situation at the beginning as a daughter nation of the British Empire, but they brought with them none of the English statute law save that which was made expressly applicable to their situation as a colony. If the principles of the English common law obtain in the greater portion of the British Empire, then is it not meet and proper that a final court of appeal be constituted so as to apply the general principles of the common and the statute law and thus have its decisions uniform? Moreover in the interpretation of a statute of great importance it would seem to be in the best interests of every portion of the empire to have a uniform interpretation of the phraseology or words of statutory enactments.
As citizens of the British Empire it is doubtful whether or not it would be in the best interests of the people to endeavour by any legislative enactments to take away, or to any great extent circumscribe, the right to an appeal to the Sovereign in Council, which is practically an appeal to the Judicial Com-19i
mittee of the Privy Council. The sovereign is said to be the fountain of justice and is constitutionally empowered to receive petitions and appeals from all his dominions and possessions, both in the Old Land and in the new, upon such regulations and conditions as may be defined by the authority of the Crown in Council. The petitions for appeal are referred to the consideration of the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council, upon whose report the decision of the sovereign is presumed to be pronounced. The Judicial Committee of the Privy Council could not, and is not permitted to, advise upon questions of general or political policy, for that is the special province of the cabinet council. Neither does it undertake to advise in criminal matters where no appeal to the Privy Council is allowed by law.
The statement that the appellate jurisdiction of the King in Council is retained for the benefit of the inhabitants of the British dominions beyond the seas, not for that of the Mother Country, cannot be gainsaid.
It secures to every British subject the right to demand redress of grievances from the throne.
When certain cases do not fall within the jurisdiction of ordinary courts of justice it provides a remedy.
It removes the influence of local prepossessions.
It is a great means of maintaining the uniformity of the law of England and those portions of the empire which derive their common law from Great Britain.
It enables suitors, if they so desire, to obtain a decision from a court which is the court of last resort so far as the British dominions are concerned, which said court is constituted of the highest judicial authority and legal capacity existing in the empire.
It is a controlling power over every judge in the empire, because he knows that his decisions are liable to be reviewed by it. Moreover, the great bulk of people in the Dominion of Canada have never exhibited a strong desire to part with the right of appeal from our courts to the king in council.
It has become the sole remaining power exercised through the crown over the British dominions.
We have ample power to establish, to abolish and to reconstitute courts of judicature and to provide for the administration of justice, but if a litigant's case is just, he should not fear its submission to a court such as is the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council.
The chief reason for the advocation of doing away with the appeal to the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council seems to
B. N. A. Act Amendment

have arisen in connection with the case of the Toronto Electric Commissioner vs Colin G. Snider and others in which the Attorney General for Canada and the Attorney General of Ontario intervened. This was an appeal taken from the decision of the Appellate Division of the High Court of Justice for the province of Ontario which, in effect, was an appeal from a judgment of Mr. Justice Mowat and Mr. Justice Orde. Briefly, the whole case had to do with and turned upon the constitutionality of the Dominion Industrial Disputes Investigation Act of 1907, 6 and 7 Edward VII, chapter 20. Mr. Justice Orde, in his judgment on an application for inj miction, gave a decision declaring the Industrial Disputes Act to be ultra vires of the Parliament of Canada, as it was an interference with property or civil rights within his province and as such was an infringement of Clause 13 of section 92 of the British North America Act, which section sets forth the exclusive legislative powers conferred upon provincial legislatures.
It is well known that section 91 of the British North America Act contains twenty-nine clauses wherein the matters which the federal parliament can exclusively legislate upon are set out. Section 92 contains sixteen clauses wherein the matters which can [DOT] be exclusively legislated upon by provincial legislatures are set out.	There is also a
general clause under Section 91 of the British North America Act which is termed a non obstante clause, wherein authority is given to the federal parliament to legislate upon all matters not exclusively given to the provincial legislatures. It has been urged by some that this non obstante clause, or the general clause, the peace, order and good government clause; gives to the Parliament of Canada authority to pass legislation infringing upon provincial rights, even though the provincial authorities have under section 92 exclusive authority. But decisions of the Privy Council have in many cases held that this general clause can only confer jurisdiction upon the federal parliament where one of the twenty-nine clauses of section 91 is in direct conflict with one of the sixteen clauses of section 92 of the British North America Act. Otherwise the clauses of section 92 mean absolutely what they say, and in so far as any right to legislate upon any particular matter can be dealt with under section 92 it cannot be interfered with by the federal parliament.
Now, Sir, so much for that. That is exactly what occurred in connection with the matter of the Industrial Disputes Investigation Act. Learned judges in Ontario held certain things;
(Mr. Martell.]
they were not unanimous, therefore it was well that it was possible to get away from any court which might have prepossessions in the matter and get the interpretation of a court quite removed from local influences, quite removed from any pressure that might otherwise be brought to bear upon it-though I do not wish to say that pressure can very well be brought upon our courts. The method of interpretation of the British North America Act has been said by the learned law lords to be as simple a method of interpretation as would be applied to an ordinary statute. The same thing may be said as regards the constitution of the Senate. I submit to the hon. member for South York that neither he nor any other person in the Dominion of Canada has the right to interfere with the constitution of the Canadian Senate unless the provinces are first consulted and their unanimous consent obtained to an amendment. The method of appointment of senators in Canada is fixed by the British North America Act and cannot be changed or interfered with in any way without the consent of all the constituents. which went to make up our charter, the British North America Act.
The cursory review which I have made in regard to the appeal to the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council applies, as I have already said, to the Senate of Canada. The government of the day, in its far-reaching, excellent and comprehensive Speech from the Throne, admits as regards the Senate that an agreement with the provinces must be had before an amendment can be made. I am afraid that if the hon. member for South York had the opportunity of laying unholy hands upon it, the appeal to the Privy Council would be abolished. In fact, his resolution is simply a subterfuge to get away from this appeal to the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council. I am not, Sir, imputing to my hon. friend the mover of the resolution any sinister object-beyond that one little object I have just mentioned. But when I hear of any person asking for the abolition of the right of appeal to the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council, I feel that it is an attempt to break away from the British connection, for the tossing buoy betrays where the anchor is hidden.
May I say in conclusion:	Let us not be
prone to sing discordant misereres against the links in the chain which bind us to the empire, for be .they of law or of sentiment, they are well forged by laws of liberty for all, and equality for all; and above all, by the law of sentiment which is sadly needed by lesser breeds without law. A3 British subjects we are citizens of no mean country,

B. N. A. Act Amendment
and from the rising of the sun until the going down thereof let us devote our energies to the upbuilding of our country, along great commercial lines, relying upon the fact that no coercive measure shall ever be applied against us by the Mother of Parliaments, and that Canada as the leading daughter in the galaxy of nations that will forever surround the British throne will always as a glorious Te Deum hymn:
Whilst the language Whilst the arts That mould a nation's soul Still cling around our hearts,
And between let oceans roll,
Our joint communion with the sun But still from either beach The voice of blood shall reach More audible than speech " We are one!"

subtopic: PROPOSED CHANGE IN METHOD OF MAKING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am in accord with the mover of this resolution (Mr. Maclean, York), as to the necessity for Canada's obtaining the right to amend her constitution, but I differ from him as to the procedure which he suggests for that purpose. I have already claimed in this House that since confederation our status had been considerably altered, but it is not my intention on this occasion to retrace at any length the developments which have occurred.
Let me state, at first, that since confederation our constitution has only been amended, at our request, and to suit our purposes, and now we may safely assert that from a constitutional point of view the Imperial parliament would never think of altering our constitution except as we so demand, and that practically the Imperial parliament has lost that right. But satisfactory as this method may be in practice, it no longer conforms to our present standing.
The equality of our status with that of any part of the British Empire has already been proclaimed on many occasions, not only by Canadians, but by most of the prominent public men of Great Britain. Canada is now a member of the League of Nations and holds therein the same standing, the same rights, as fully sovereign nations. She has in the assembly of the league her own representatives enjoying all the rights of any of the other members. In the treaty of Versailles Canada appears as a unit, separate from that of Great Britain, though under the same king. She now negotiates alone her commercial treaties with foreign nations, and she signs these treaties by her own representatives, acting in the name of the King, but having received their full powers from him at the
instance and under the direction of the Canadian cabinet. AH these prerogatives are now fully acknowledged as belonging to us, but they are incompatible with the control which Great Britain can, theoretically, and in the eyes of foreign nations, exercise over us if she is the superior authority or the power which alone has the right to alter our constitution. Moreover, Australia, Sooth Africa and Ireland, now enjoy the right to amend their constitution, and Canada cannot continue to occupy the inferior itank of the dominion which is not empowered to exercise the rights which belong to the other dominions.
For these reasons it is necessary that we should take steps to obtain the right of altering our constitution by an internal pioeedure entirely under our control.
But the constitution of Canada has a special feature; it is the result of a pact between the different provinces of Canada; it has this character, at least for the four original members of the confederation. For these four provinces it is a covenant or agreement, and it follows that no amendment or alteration of importance can be made to this covenant without the participation and consent of the parties to it. The other provinces which came in later entered this covenant of their own free wild, and they should be entitled to the same privileges as the original members. It follows that no alteration of an important character can be made to the British North America Act, our constitution, unless it meets with the approval of the provinces which compose the confederation.
This conventional character of our constitution was also a feature of that of the Commonwealth of Australia, and if you refer to its constitution you will find that the right to alter the constitution has been surrounded by a number of protective measures, which preserve adequately the rights of each of the states which compose the commonwealth. The alteration of its constitution is made by a law, passed by an absolute majority in each of the two houses of parliament, and submitted to the electors qualified to vote for the election of members of the house of representatives, in each of the different states of the confederation, and this amendment comes into force if approved by the majority of the states and by the majority of all the electors who voted. It provides also, that in case of disagreement between the two houses of parliament, the Governor General may submit to the electora any proposed amendment passed twice after an interval of at least three months by any one of these houses.
B. N. A. Act Amendment

In Australia, as in Canada, there are some fundamental rights which must be preserved with yet more care. We would hold here as sacred rights:	The territorial limits of the
provinces:	The proportion of representation
of each province:	The rights which are attributed by the British North America Act to the provinces, particularly in matters of education:	The privileges of minorities; and
some others.
In Australia no alteration to the constitution which may in any way affect any of the rights which are considered fundamental can come into force as to each separate state unless it has received the approval of the majority of the electors in that state. So in Canada, our constitution should be so drafted that any alteration, which might affect some of these fundamental rights should necessarily receive the approval of the legislature of each province to which it may apply.
For these reasons, though I am in favour of the principle of the resolution, I cannot accept it as drafted, and I must register my vote against it. Moreover, I submit that any attempt to obtain the right to amend our constitution must be the subject of a conference between the provinces, and must meet *with the approval of each of the component parts of Canada.

subtopic: PROPOSED CHANGE IN METHOD OF MAKING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise in opposition to this resolution. I believe there is no demand for this legislation. Furthermore, I believe that if this legislature did have the power that is asked for here, it would sound the death knell in this country of the basis of confederation; it would sound the death knell of minorities; it would sound the death knell of provincial rights, and more especially of municipal rights, and we must remember that there has been a very large investment by municipalities from coast to coast throughout this country in public utilities. Now, there is no demand for this legislation; nobody is asking for it. I am an Irishman but I should be sorry to see thi3 country with a constitution such as Ireland has to-day. They have the right over there to make and unmake their constitution. What does the resolution of my hon. friend ask for:
The parliament of the Dominion may amend the said British North America Act when it may see fit to do so.
Under suoh provision as that would not this parliament have the right to deprive the provinces of the powers which they at present enjoy under section 92 of the British North America Act? Is it proposed that this Dominion should be able to brush aside with a

wave of the hand, the constitutional rights of the provinces and municipalities throughout this country? Let me give an illustration of what I mean. The municipalities and provinces in many cases are doing more to solve practical problems than is this parliament. The other day the leader of this government stated that the Dominion had nothing to do with the question of unemployment under the British North America Act. At present the control of the banking institutions of the country, of immigration, of transportation, of the tariff, and of the right to enter into international agreements, is vested in this parliament, and it ought to relieve the provinces and the municipalities of the problem of caring for unemployment. I am very much surprised that the hon. member for South York (Mr. Maclean), an advocate of public ownership as he is, in view of the fact that the city of Toronto from which he comes has made an investment of $125,000,000 in light, power, and transportation; in view of the fact that his constituency has been beneficially affected by these enterprises, should' move such a resolution as this. Because, if the amendment to the British North America Act which he proposes had been in operation in Canada, there would have been no such developments in connection with light, power and transportation as have taken place in Ontario. The power to build, run and control these utilities would be usurped and interfered with by the Dominion and it would be possible for the Dominion by interference to wipe them out in the twinkling of an eye.
My hon. friend (Mr. Maclean, York) wants to know whether Canada is a sovereign state, whether it is a nation, and whether we can make and unmake our own constitution. No, Canada is not a sovereign state, and it is a good thing that it is not. Notwithstanding the fact that we have the right to sign halibut treaties, and other treaties, we are not a sovereign state. We are a nation in name only. We are dependent-just as is Australia to which dominion my hon. friend ascribed the possession of so much power-on the fleet of the Mother Country. Here we are talking about an amendment to the British North America Act, and in time of trouble we are the first to look to the old Motherland across the seas for protection and for the maintenance of the maritime freedom which we enjoy. And notwithstanding this protection we are content to sponge on the hard earnings of the British taxpayer for our maritime freedom without doing anything to relieve him of the burden. In this respect we are unlike the Commonwealth of Australia. What is their

B. N. A. Act Amendment
attitude in this matter? They have a fleet of their own and contribute to maritime freedom. Let me quote from wtiat the Prime Minister of Australia, Right Hon. S. M. Bruce, said as reported in volume 5, number 4, Journal of the Parliaments of the Empire, issued in October, 1924:
At no time throughout her history had Australia been in a position to provide for her own national defence. To-day, as in the past, they were dependent upon the protection afforded to them by Great Britain. They had to recognize that fact. It was useless for anybody to maintain that if they were an independent nation, with no connection with the British Empire, they would be in a position to protect themselves. The certainty that they could not defend themselves would be a considerable incentive to any country to take action against them. They had the most wonderful unprotected white man's country in the world, with only five and a half to six millions of people inhabiting it. Looking round the world, however, they saw teeming millions in other countries, and knowing the rate at which their populations were increasing, they in Australia recognized the difficulties with which those countries were faced in finding an outlet for their people. " Few of us " said Mr. Bruce, " fail to recognize that Australia, undefended, would be a great temptation to any country." We all subscribe to the " White Australia " quality, which we say shall never, under any circumstances be abandoned. We intend to keep this country white and not allow its people to be faced with the problems that at present are practically insoluble in many other parts of the world. . . . It is true that, in the past, our right to assert this policy has never been seriously challenged, but it has enjoyed immunity from challenge because we are part of the British Empire, and have had the whole force of Britain behind us throughout our history.
I am afraid there is altogether too much talk in this country with respect to abolishing appeals to the Privy Council which is calculated to have the effect of weakening the ties which unite us to the Mother Country. I am afraid that legislation such as is proposed here would make it possible to encroach upon provincial rights, and in the case of the province of Ontario reduce to scrap many valuable public undertakings. In a word it would be possible to reduce the provincial legislature and the municipalities of a province to the mere status of a county council. The highest judicial court in the empire recently gave a judgment on the Industrial Disputes Investigation Act holding matters wholly provincial in their scope and activity and affecting property and civil rights, employer and employee, as matters for the provinces and not for the Dominion under trade and commerce. I do not wish to criticise the judgment of the Ontario court of appeal, I would not say anything derogatory with respect to it; but I must express the opinion that the judgment of the Privy Council removed one of the most deadly menaces to provincial rights in affirming that the provincial court of appeal was wrong in upholding, as it did, the Industrial Disputes Act. That law was held to be a
bad piece of legislation by the Dominion by the highest court in the British Empire. On the other hand the judgment of the Ontario court of appeal would have absolutely destroyed provincial and municipal rights which we have enjoyed since the British North America Act first came into force. That judgment of the Ontario court of appeal has been upset by the highest court in the realm. This decision will stand for all time as a shining example of how the Privy Council protects 1he rights of minorities and provincial and municipal rights as well when threatened by the Dominion. We have had many statutes enacted by the Dominion tending to invade the provincial field. We have had the Combines Act which was more ornamental than useful. Since that act was enacted I am not aware that there has been a single prosecution instituted successfully under it.
Reverting to Australia, I may say that the commonwealth has appreciated its position much better than Canada has, and has established a fleet to protect its shores. According to the report of the Canadian Minister of National Defence Canada's expenditure on defence is only $1.46 per head of the population. Great Britain's expenditure for this purpose is $23.04; while Australia pays $3.30. If we are a nation, and this resolution passes, I suppose we should have the right to go to war, with the toy navy which we now have. The only thing this parliament appears to be ready to declare war on is on the rights of the provinces. That very clearly is what was done when the Industrial Disputes Investigation Act was enacted.
In the Old Country the press has been discussing the resolution of my hon. friend, and among others the Manchester Guardian. Well, I do not think there is any newspaper in the British Empire which knows less of Canadian affairs than the Manchester Guardian. In the present instance it is sympathetic towards the abolition of appeals to the Privy Council which would weaken the ties which unite Canada to the Motherland, because the Privy Council to-dfey is one of the remaining links binding Canada to the Mother Country. I think we are doing altogether too much to weaken the ties and relations between Canada and the Motherland.
It is said we can make our own treaties. I hope the day is far distant when Canada will be making its own treaties, because I think the treaties which are made by the Mother Country for Canada stand out by themselves and are beneficial to Canada. It is said we should have a Canadian ambassador at Washington. I may say I am opposed to that.
B. N. A. Act Amendment

That is another way of weakening the ties which bind Canada to the Mother Country, and is not in keeping with the spirit of the British North America Act which is one of the remaining links which 'bind together Canada and the Old Land. Some people want to abolish the offices of Governor General and Lieutenant Governor. I hope these offices will not be abolished, because they are two of the few remaining links which bind Canada to tihe Motherland.
Before any resolution of this character is passed by parliament I think the provinces should be consulted. The provinces are a part >of confederation. Under the British North America Act, sections 91 and 92, they have been given a written constitution and they should be consulted before any change is made in the act. Before we make 'any such change we should have a vote of the people, and no one is asking for a vote that I know of, or any change in the act as it stands to-day. As a matter of fact, Mr. Speaker, we are living in an age in which changes to our constitution will have the effect of weakening the ties which bind Canada to the Motherland. Many prohibitory laws are being passed. We seem to be living in an age when prohibitory legislation is a fad, too many prohibitory laws are being passed, and I think there is too much tinkering with the constitution. Nowadays people seem anxious to discipline their neighbours, but do not want to discipline themselves.
One of the reasons for the present resolution was the decision given in the Privy Council in the appeal of the Toronto Hydro-Electric Commissioners in a case involving a labour dispute, and it is held by some that the judgment declares the whole Industrial Disputes Investigation Act ultra vires of the Dominion parliament. I say that as far as that act dealt with Dominion matters, as long as it stayed within its own field and looked after the federal field and the rights of Dominion employees, it was all very well and proper. As long as the act was kept in its own federal sphere and 'applied it to the subject for which it was intended' under section 91 of the British North America Act-that is works declared to be for the general advantage of Canada, which came under the jurisdiction of this parliament, such as Post Office employees, railway employees and federal employees- it was perfectly valid. So far as that act went I believe it did some good work, although it has not been a success in some other ways.
The bill was framed by the hon. presiding officer of this chamber (Mr. Lemieux) a gentleman who has been a long time in public

life in this country, and who has all his life done a great deal to promote provincial good will and to advocate the principles of fair dealing between man and man throughout the country. The worthy author of this bill spent his life in the sendee of this country, and he never intended that that act should be utilized and used the way it has been, namely to stray out of the Dominion field and enter into the provincial and municipal fields and undertake to do work which it was not intended to do. The act was intended to function so far as it applied to federal matters under section 91 of the British North America Act, and so far as it applied also to any provincial works which were undertaken which were declared to be works for the general advantage of Canada. But when it left the federal field and invaded the provincial and municipal fields and dealt with municipal utilities-light, and power and many other things-and sought to constitute itself a court of appeal from the cities or towns, or a court of appeal in the province, then it crossed the border and entered a field where it did not belong.
I think the judgment given by Lord Haldane was sound where he deals with the matter of the protection of provincial and municipal rights in this country. I may say that the legislature of the province of Ontario is complaining, and I think they have good cause to complain, that this federal body is encroaching on their rights and dealing with matters which come under the provincial jurisdiction. I first refer to the St. Lawrence development, where eastern Ontario is affected. There was an application before- the government to build up the Morrisburg dam. Under the British North America Act as it stands to-day the surplus waters subject to the rights o-f navigation belong to the province and the banks and rapids and bed of international streams. That is one constitutional question of which Ontario is asking for some solution.
Another question in which there is trouble under the British North America Act in the province I come from is the question of insurance. That has been before the Privy Council on several occasions, and the Prime Minister of Ontario said that Ottawa had gone out of its way to veto provincial legislation when there was no occasion for it. I think there was no reason for interference in regard to the question of light, power and insurance problems of the province. There is another serious conflict regarding insurance, although the province of Ontario recovered a judgment before the Privy Council twice protecting the legislation we passed. I may say

B. N. A. Act Amendment
that among other matters affecting the province are the succession duties and the revenues of the province, and the control of the water. powers of the province. If this amendment carries it would interfere with all these matters. I say there is no demand for the legislation. Nobody is asking for it, and I do not know what good it would do if we did have the legislation. What we want during the present session is that parliament should solve some practical problems concerning the people of this country at this time. One most important matter is unemployment and another is the light and power question of this Dominion. We have many other practical problems to deal with instead of taking up a question which the people are not bothering their heads about.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: PROPOSED CHANGE IN METHOD OF MAKING
speechtext:
Any proposal affecting the constitution of Canada is by its nature of considerable importance, and the mere fact that such an experienced politician as my hon. friend from York (Mr. Maclean) has fathered this resolution is a strong indication that the subject matter of this resolution attracts a substantial measure of public attention. I desire merely to point out some of the difficulties which are in the way of the proposal submitted by my hon. friend. If I do not agree with him in many of his statements, I do agree at least with the statement that he made that there is no difficulty whatever in this connection with the Mother Country. My hon. friend stated, and repeated, that we could have that right if we asked for it, and he is absolutely right. I think that the language of some of the resolutions which I have read in the newspapers as having been adopted by associations in this country is rather unfortunate, because it conveys the impression that the Mother Country is refusing something, and that we ought to claim the right to amend our own constitution. The question, as my hon. friend rightly said, is not and cannot be one between Great Britain and Canada. It is one and might be a difficulty between this parliament and the provinces if there is any conflict in that regard.
It is true that in Australia, South Africa, New Zealand and in the Irish Free State, those dominions can, subject to many restrictions, amend their constitution. Not so with Canada. The British North America Act says itself that the Parliament of Great Britain merely enacted, put into a statute, the wish of the people of the provinces of Canada. It is of our making, and it is after an understanding between the bodies representing the provinces of Canada at that time.
There were many obstacles in the way of achieving confederation. Everybody who knows something of the history of Canada knows what some at least of those obstacles were. The country was on the verge of civil strife. During the two years which preceded the Quebec resolutions, not less than four cabinets succeeded each other at the head of the affairs of Canada. The provinces got together; they tried to effect an understanding and they effected one. In the language of Sir John A. Macdonald, the very pact of confederation bears on its face all the marks of a compromise. The provinces relinquished some of the powers which were theirs and they retained for themselves other powers. The powers which they relinquished they relinquished subject to conditions which were put into confederation, some of those conditions being more or less important, others essential, and without such conditions confederation would not have taken place. They tried to combine federal strength with local freedom of action. Everything that was private, domestic, home rule, the provinces kept to themselves, and they saw to it that their powers in that regard should never be interfered with. It is to be noted that in the British North America Act, they have the right to amend those provisions which concern their own constitution, except as regards the office of the Lieutenant-Governor. Not so in the case of any of the provisions concerning the federal parliament; and there were reasons for that. If confederation was a pact, an agreement, is it possible for one of the parties to the agreement, or rather for the body which resulted from the agreement, to amend, to alter the conditions of that pact without consulting and without securing the consent of the parties to the original agreement?

subtopic: PROPOSED CHANGE IN METHOD OF MAKING
speechtext: What is the rule in the United States?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: PROPOSED CHANGE IN METHOD OF MAKING
speechtext:
The United States never had the same position as had the provinces at the time of confederation. As regards the United States as well as Australia, New Zealand and South Africa, they all agreed at the time of the enactment of the statute creating their constitution that they would have the right to alter it. They possess that right because it was made one of the conditions of the statute constituting them a state. Not so with Canada, because there were special conditions and difficulties in the way. I ask my hon. friend this question. Confederation was achieved and the new parliament was opened in 1867. Does he believe that two years aftewards, in 1869, for in-
B. N. A. Act Amendment

stance, this parliament could have fairly and reasonably amended the British 5 p.m. North America Act or have asked the Imperial parliament to amend it without the consent of the lour original provinces? Could he fairly say that that could have been done two years after the opening of this parliament? If it could not be done at that time, could it be done twenty-five years afterwards, or even fifty years afterwards, without the consent of the contracting parties in the pact of confederation?
I want to convey to the House one or two points and I desire every one of my colleagues not to lose sight of this. First, the British North America Act itself is not only the charter of the Dominion of Canada; it is just as much the charter of the provinces of Canada. We derive our powers from the British North America Act; so do the provinces. They have no constitution other than the British North America Act; all their powers they derive from that act. Would it then be fair for us to arrogate to ourselves the right to change the act which is just as much the constitution of the provinces as it is our own? Second, my hon. friend speaks of protection to minorities. That is not the only thing in the British North America Act in which the provinces are interested. They have all their powers which they have kept to themselves and which have been agreed by everybody to be their powers. Have we a right to amend the constitution without their consent, in the way, for instance, of taking away from them some of the powers which have been theirs since confederation.

speechtext:
This parliament would
have that power in respect of all provinces excepting the four that originally1 entered confederation.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: PROPOSED CHANGE IN METHOD OF MAKING
speechtext:
I do not agree with my hon. friend in that regard. The other provinces came later into a joint confederation, but they have the same status, powers and rights as the original four provinces and they should be consulted just as much as any other province if any substantial change is asked as regards the British North America Act.
Third, within their sphere the provinces enjoy the powers of self-government just as much as the Dominion parliament does, and if so, surely the Dominion parliament cannot take upon itself the right to change a statute which gives to those provinces the powers which they enjoy.
Perhaps I could not do better than quote three of . the leading propositions given by Professor Lefroy in The Canadian Constitution. They are propositions Nos. 2, 51 and 59, reading as follows:
(Mr. Lapointe.]
2. Although the British North America Act was founded upon the Quebec resolutions, and so must be accepted as embodying a treaty of union between the provinces, yet when once enacted it constituted a wholly new point of departure, and established the dominion and provincial governments with definite powers and duties both alike derived from it as their source.
51. The object of the British North America Act was neither to weld the provinces into one nor to subordinate provincial governments to a central authority, but to create a federal government in which they should all be represented and entrusted with the exclusive administration of affairs in which they have a common interest, each province retaining its independence and autonomy.
59. The Dominion parliament cannot either expressly or impliedly take away from or give to the provincial legislatures the power which the Imperial act does or does not give their, and the same is the case, mutatis mutandis, with the provincial legislatures.
If, Mr. Speaker, you agree with me, and if you agree with Professor Lefroy in the proposition which I have just stated, surely the conclusion is that we cannot ask for power to alter, without the consent of the provinces, the constitution which is their own constitution as well as it is ours. It also follows that if it is to be considered as a treaty, surely we cannot alter its provisions without at least seeking the consent of the other parties to that treaty.
Now, has it been considered as a treaty? I heard it suggested some time ago that this idea at confederation of a treaty is an antiquated idea. Maybe it is. But, Mr. Speaker, truth does not cease to be truth when it gets old; an old truth is always true. You cannot prevent facts from being facts whether you like them or not. I have here the Debates of the Parliament of Canada on Confederation. What did Sir John Macdonald think about it?
