Perhaps my hon. friend will allow me to proceed and I will answer him later. Here is what Sir John Macdonald
said, page 15-*
In answer to the member for Carleton-
That is, when the Quebec resolutions were laid on the table.
-the government desired to say that they presented the scheme as a whole, and they would exert all the influence they could bring to bear in the way of argument to induce the House to adopt the scheme without alteration, and for the simple reason that the scheme was not one framed by the government of Canada or by the government of Nova Scotia, but was in the nature of a treaty settled between the

B. N. A. Act Amendment
different colonies, each clause of which had been fully discussed, and which had been agreed to by a system of mutual compromise.
In the speech he made a few days afterwards, when moving the adoption of confederation,-page 31-he said:
I trust the scheme will be assented to as a whole.
I am sure this House will not seek to alter it in its unimportant details; and, if altered in any important provisions, the result must be that the whole will be set aside, and we must begin de novo. If any important changes are made, everyone of the colonies will feel itself absolved from the implied obligation to deal with it as a treaty, each province will feel itself at liberty to amend it ad libitum so as to suit its own views and interests; in fact, the whole of our labours will have been for naught, and we will have to renew our negotiations with all the colonies for the purpose of establishing some new scheme.
Sir George Etienne Cartier, Hon. George Brown,	and	aM	the	other Fathers of
Confederation used similar language. May I be permitted to quote a few words from the speech .made on	that occasion by Hon.
D'Arcy McGee, the centenary of whose birth will be celebrated in a few months? He said, at page 136:
We assembled under authority of that dispatch, and acted under the sanction it gave. Everything we did was done in form and with propriety, and the result of our proceedings is the document that has been submitted to the Imperial government as well as to this House, and which we speak of here as a treaty. And that there may be no doubt about our position in regard to that document we say, question it you may, reject it you may, or accept it you may, but alter it you may not. It is beyond your power, or our power, to alter it. There is not a sentence-aye, or even a word-you can alter without desiring to throw out the document. Alter it, and we know at once what you mean-you thereby declare yourselves anti-unionists. On this point I repeat after all my hon. friends who have already spoken, for one party to alter a treaty, is of course, to destroy it. Let us be frank with each other; you who do not like our work, nor do you like us who stand by it; clause by clause, line by line, and letter by letter. Oh! But this clause ought to run thus, and this other clause thus. Does any hon. member seriously think that any treaty in the world between five separate provinces ever gave full and entire satisfaction on every point to every party? Does any hon. member seriously expect to have a constitutional act framed to his order or my order, or any man's order? No, Sir, I am sure no legislator at least since Anacharsis Clootz was " Attorney-General of the Human Race " ever expected such ideal perfection.
There was some Irish wit in the last words of Mr. McGee. Since confederation what have our own statesmen thought about this matter? In 1906-7 Sir Wilfrid Laurier said, and his remarks will be found at page 2199 of the Hansard of that session:
In parliament here we can do as we please; we are in the majority; but are the members of this House prepared to ;:ay that if a. y province finds itself aggrieved by the terms of confederation, which have been accepted by all the provinces, they will ask the British parliament to alter the constitution in the way desired by that particular province? Such a
course might be followed by very serious consequences. Confederation is a compact, made originally by four provinces, but adhered to by all the nine provinces who have entered it, and I submit to the judgment of this House and to the best consideration of its members, that this compact should not be lightly altered. It should be altered only for adequate cause, and after the provinces themselves have had an opportunity to pass judgment on the same.
Sir Robert Borden-then	leader of the
opposition-speaking	in the same debate,
used the following words:
I agree with what has been said by the right hon. gentleman regarding the undesirability of lightly amending the terms of our constitution and am inclined to agree with him on the necessity of some consultation with the provinces, although of course all the provinces are represented here. But inasmuch as this is a federal compact which we are asked to vary, it is only right that each province should be consulted and its decision given, in the right of its separate entity.
At that time there had been an interprovincial conference which considered the question of increasing the subsidies to the provinces, and after an agreement between those provinces an address was voted by both houses of this parliament for the purpose of amending the British North America Act to give to the provinces an increased subsidy. This address was submitted to the Imperial parliament. The Premier of British Columbia, the late Sir Richard McBride, went to London at the time-not that he was opposed to the amendment altering the provisions of the British North America Act and giving an increased subsidy to the provinces, but his objection was that British Columbia should have more than was given to her under the agreement and under the act which was submitted to the Imperial parliament at the request of the Dominion of Canada. I wish to quote from the remarks of the Secretary of State for the Colonies at the time, Mr. Winston Churchill, the present Chancellor of the Exchequer, just to show that the interpretation given to the confederation pact by the public men of the Dominion was also the interpretation given to it by imperial public men. On submitting the bill for its first reading Mr. Churchill said:
On the other hand, he would be very sorry if it were thought that the action which His Majesty's government had decided to take meant that they had decided to establish as a precedent that whenever there was a difference on a constitutional question between the federal government and one of the provinces,
He was referring to the objection of British Columbia.
-the Imperial government would always be prepared to accept the federal point of view as against the provincial. In deference to the representations of British Columbia the words "final and unalterable" applying to the revised scale had been omitted from the bill.

B. N. A. Act Amendment
His language was still more explicit on the second reading of the bill. He said: I quote from page 753 of the British Hansard of 1907:
Tlie hon. baronet, the member for the city of
London, asked why the bill came here at all. The British North America Act is the fundamental act governing the constitution of the Dominion of Canada, and different prime ministers of Canada voluntarily entered into that union. Adherence to the union was something in the nature of a. treaty, and when an alteration in the basis of the treaty is made, as it is by the revised schedule of subventions proposed, it was felt desirable by all the prime ministers in conference that such a matter should be ratified by the Imperial parliament in the most formal way.
That was the interpretation that was accepted by every interested person in Canada, and I submit to my hon. friend the mover of the resolution that it is even to-day the interpretation that is given by the public men of Canada in the provinces.
Two or three years ago one of my predecessors in the Department of Justice, Right Hon. Mr. Doherty, had contemplated some legislation along this line, and he communicated with the various provinces. The correspondence is of a confidential character, but I may say that Mr. Doherty and all the attorneys general who answered his letter were o; the same opinion, that nothing of this kind could be done without the consent of the provinces. The present Attorney General of Ontario was not then in the provincial government, but I have his opinion in a letter he wrote me last year concerning proposed legislation of this parliament. This is what Mr. Nickle says:
I do not need to remind you that the British North
America Act was a product of representatives from all the provinces as such, and not as representatives to a Dominion parliament. The government of this province is of opinion that the Dominion parliament should not act in the matter of obtaining constitutional changes, without the sanction of the provinces to its proposals to the Imperial parliament.

I repeat, Mr. Speaker, that if the British North America Act is a covenant, is of the nature of a treaty the provisions of which were essential for the acceptance of the whole scheme, have we the right to ask to be enabled to alter it without the consent of those who were parties to the agreement?

By the men of to-day,
yes. I am not one of those who are riveted to the past and who are prepared to deny to our children the liberty of the future, but those changes the necessity for which may be seen as a result of our experience of sixty years cannot be made unless you proceed in a legal and constitutional way; they cannot be made arbitrarily; they cannot be made only at the will and at the request of the Dominion parliament; but those who are just as much interested as the Dominion parliament in this matter must have their say, must be consulted, and must give their assent.
I have read a very interesting work by Sir Clifford Sifton on this very subject. Sir Clifford is a constitutional authority, and has given much thought to this matter. He believes in the fullest degree of autonomy for Canada, and his work and his lectures are very interesting and very weighty. He admits as does Mr. Kennedy of Toronto university, and all the constitutional writers, that the British North America Act is a pact and must be treated as such. Mr. Kennedy, who has
written a very important book on the constitution of Canada, and who, like my hon. friend from South York (Mr. Maclean) would like Canada to have the power to amend its constitution, admits that the British North America Act is a covenant and a pact, and he sees the difficulty in the way. Sir Clifford Sifton too, in his work, admits that the British North America Act is a pact and must be treated as such, and what does he suggest? He suggests a conference of delegates elected by the popular vote of Canada. Parliament would divide Canada into a certain number of districts which would elect delegates to that conference by way of proportional representation, and those delegates would revise or frame a constitution for Canada, which would be submitted to the people for approval.
The other plan he suggests is that a parliamentary committee should be formed to which would be called all the men who are constitutional lawyers in Canada, and all those who are interested in this matter, to give their views. That committee would revise the constitution, but its findings would be subject to a vote of the people of Canada.
There is much to be said perhaps in favour of both these schemes, but they are defective in one main, principal point. Neither of these bodies suggested by Sir Clifford Sifton would represent all the parties to the pact of confederation. The body or conference or gathering which might be entrusted with the work of revising our constitution must be a body in which the provinces, as such, and not otherwise, shall be represented, as well as this Dominion parliament. That is the point upon which I differ with Sir Clifford Sifton.

We have had within the last thirty or forty years the development of the great Canadian west; and some of us who are from the west, representing peoples of the west who were not living in the country at that time, representing constituencies in provinces which were not originally in confederation, feel that our development ought not to be forever tied because of certain legislation which was drawn up fifty or sixty years ago. Past generations

The letter killeth but the spir't giveth life
Who then is best fitted to interpret, in the light of modern conditions, these laws of fifty or sixty years ago? Not, I submit, the men who live across the Atlantic, but the men who are living here in Canada and dealing with the everyday affairs of our Canadian people.
The Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe), in his speech, referred to some words that I used the other day in another connection, "Where there is a will there is a way". He seems to think that these words, which most of us learned in our school days and were then considered to be quite orthodox, carried some very sinister meaning; they remind him of the Germans. The minister referred to the fact that there were obstacles in the way of achieving confederation. born and of several generations of Canadians, and as such, a Canadian of the Canadians, I want to protest against any narrowness of that kind. Oh, no. I am not suggesting anything of the kind. The Minister of Justice is not responsible for the statement in question; it emanated from the hon. member for Fort William and Rainy River (Mr. Manion). I would urge that the only way we can maintain confederation is to insist absolutely upon justice for all, for the newcomer as well as for the old timer, for the westerner as well as for the easterner, for those parts of the country which entered confederation more recently as well as for those that entered it when the British North America Act was passed. I believe in federation, I believe in still wider federation-I believe we all hope for an ultimate world federation-but these things can be accomplished only as we maintain a very large measure of home rule-and we ought to have home rule here in Canada. In order to obviate the difficulties that seem to face the Minister of Justice and several other members with regard to this resolution I beg leave to move the following amendment seconded by Mr. Shaw:
That the resolution be amended as follows: by adding the following words after thr word "Dominion" in the first line of clause 2 thereof, to wit:
Upon first obtaining the consent of all the provinces of Canada.
I think this will meet the objection raised by the Minister of Justice and the hon. member for St. Hyacinthe-Rouville (Mr. Morin). If that amendment were adopted we would not have any action whatever until all the provinces had consented thereto. Moreover, in accordance with the original motion, there is the further safeguard that there would be no power to pass any amendment affecting the rights guaranteed in the said act to minorities. Surely such a resolution, if it is not harmless-that is the only possible trouble with it-would absolutely safeguard the fundamental principles laid down in the British North America Act.

The resolution amended in that way would be a great improvement on the resolution moved by the hon. member for South York (Mr. Maclean), but there is this objection: I think it might be possible to get the assent of the provinces to such a change being made in the British North America Act with the amendment suggested by my hon. friend: that this parliament be enabled to amend the constitution after having secured the assent of all the provinces to the amendment made by parliament, but I say even to get this amendment before the Imperial parliament you must have the consent of the provinces. That is my objection to the proposal, even as amended by my hon. friend from Centre Winnipeg (Mr. Woodsworth). It becomes a much fairer proposal, but the provinces have a right to be consulted before this is asked from the British parliament; and I submit even with this amendment the Parliament of Canada has not the constitutional right to pass an address to the Imperial parliament to amend the Act of Confederation without first submitting the proposal to the provinces.

I agree very largely with what my hon. friend the Minister of Justice has said. I think he has made it perfectly clear what the real situation is, in so far as parliament is concerned, in so far as the provinces are concerned, and in so far as provincial rights are concerned, apart altogether from any question of minority rights. There is a good deal more reserved in the British North America Act than the mere question of minorities; and with what my hon. friend has said in that regard I absolutely agree. But I would like to get a little more clearly defined what all the trouble is. What are we talking about? What grievances do we want wiped out? How far do we advance ourselves to clarify the issue by adopting this or any other resolution? Let us go a little bit further. Is there really anything in that of great importance at a time when, as the hon. member for Centre Winnipeg (Mr. Woodsworth) says, we are chiefly concerned as to how people are going to live to-day? Is there anything in it of sufficient importance to warrant taking up very much time? How does this matter come up at any rate? There is no dispute certainly as between England and Canada, but a dispute having regard to the maintenance of provincial institutions in Ontario. That is what the dispute is about and nothing else. Does anyone here think it is worth while for a minute referring to the provinces the question of the settlement of that jurisdiction? It is settled. It always was settled. I have heard something said in the House to-day about the Privy Council. Well the Privy Council did not rnaike that law. We all understood the law. I am speaking now as a matter of recollection, but I think it was in connection with the trouble at Edmonton concerning a municipal activity, when we were about to do the same thing as was done in Toronto, and our own Department of Justice advised the government that the step ought not to be taken, that it would raise at once an issue under which the Dominion would be putting its hand directly on a municipal institution, and when you put your hand upon a municipal institution you are affecting something which is entirely read out of the jurisdiction of parliament in so many words. In connection with a municipal institution which is carried on for the purpose of getting cheap utilities and cheap light and power, it is idle to say that it has to do with the matter of Trade and Commerce, when the very act dealing with the matter, the British North America Act, says that municipal institutions are absolutely and entirely reserved to the province. It is not new law at all. It is the law as given to the preceding government by its own legal department. Just so long as we kept out of the field where our own federal officers told us we could not go we had a very useful act. Just as soon as we put our hands where we were told we had no right to go, we are told, and properly told, in effect that our own legal advisers were correct.
The thing now for us to do is to talk this over with the provincial parliaments, not talking about getting through any general resolution which will take us really nowhere, because no general resolution-and everybody knows that is perfectly correct-will ever be consented to by the provinces. Why should they consent? Why should they consent to

an abridgement of their rights by one single jot or tittle, until they know what they are dealing with? If we have concrete principles to submit to the provinces, there is some sense in submitting them; but we will never have any hope of getting through a general amendment to the British North America Act which will tell us that the sovereign power over these provinces is in this Dominion.
What is really the trouble? In Canada at present we are wasting a great deal of time just talking about constitutional questions, theoretical questions. Why are we doing so? Is there anything after all, about our connection with the Old Motherland that we are ashamed of or want to change? Whom are we trying to please? It is often said that these things do not hurt or do not matter. They do not at home. We know Derfectly well that some of us like to take a certain amount of intellectual exercise, just showing how wise we are about this problem and that problem, no matter what it is or what claim is put forward on behalf of Canada, looking to enlarged powers as against the Mother Country, and we know that the great bulk of the Canadian people are only too well satisfied to let things rest just as they are; that they desire to maintain the British connection, and that they are .proud of their connection with the British Empire. If they are not and if we are not doing this merely as a form of intellectual exercise, what is the teal trouble? What real grievance have we as regards our position in the British Empire as it stands to-day? Are we not free enough? speechtext: The House resumed, from February 18, consideration of the proposed resolution of Mr. Maclean (York), and the proposed amendment thereto of Mr. Woodsworth.

subtopic: PROPOSED CHANGE IN METHOD OF MAKING AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the time the House rose yesterday I think we were all pretty well agreed at least upon one thing, and that is that it had been well demonstrated by the hon. Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) that no good purpose could be served by passing the resolution, but that on the other hand mischief might well result from it. I am disposed, however, to think that a good deal of good perhaps will come of the discussion which this resolution has forced upon the House.
The first thing that seems to be quite clearly established from what the hon. Minister of Justice has told us is that all our constitutional difficulties are of our own making. That is the first proposition which I think is absolutely and amply established.
The second proposition is that all such difficulties arise owing to the infringement of rights, either provincial or dominion. I take it that there can be no dispute whatever with that proposition.
There is a third proposition, which I hope will find just as immediate acceptance in the minds of all hon. gentlemen, and which I believe requires no demonstration; and that is that Canada to-day is content, and well content, to remain as Canada is, a part, and I hope a part of constantly increasing influence for good, but still a part, of the greatest political entity the world has yet seen, and I think will ever see-the British Empire. I hope again there is absolutely no room for doubt on that.
If we get these three propositions firmly in our minds, if they are really understood by our people, this will have been a very useful discussion.
Now, as to the first proposition. It seems to me that very little need be said in connection with that, namely that all our con-
B.N.A. Act Amendment

stitutional difficulties are difficulties of our own making. I do not think there was any member in the House who was not convinced and carried by the speech of the hon. Minister of Justice in that regard. It was clear, and he had a wealth of authority for every proposition that he advanced, indeed the fact is well known by everybody, or ought to be, that bur constitution, complain about it as we rtiay, is of our own making.
The second proposition I think is equally clear, and that is that the constitutional troubles which we have arise over questions which are founded upon infringement of provincial rights on the one hand or of Dominion rights on the other. Can there be any dispute about that? It is such an important thing, particularly at this present time that we should all thoroughly understand that our constitutional difficulties are difficulties each with the other-not only difficulties of our own making, but difficulties each with the other, and they never should be looked upon or made use of for one minute by anybody as a reason for creating discontent with Canada's status within the British Empire. Now is there any doubt about it? Every constitutional difficulty which we have is a difficulty which is founded either upon an infringement of provincial rights by the Dominion or upon an infringement of Dominion rights by the provinces. The whole history of decided cases shows that. What claim does Great Britain or the empire make to-day upon anything Canadian? What objection does either make to any Canadian activity? We all know there is absolutely none.
What are the two questions which have given rise to this issue to-day, which has taken, I think, a most mistaken form? The more immediate one is what has happened to the Industrial Disputes Investigation Act. But what did we learn there? We learned nothing new but something we had always known, and that is that municipal institutions belong to the provinces and not to the Dominion. Is there any hon. gentleman in this House who would like to take the responsibility of declaring negatively on that principle? Is there any issue about it, is there anything to confer about in so far as municipal institutions are concerned? So far at any rate no public man in Canada has been bold enough to make that claim. Municipal institutions are the creations and the work of the provincial legislatures, which are all-powerful in that respect, and the act carrying out the agreement between those legislatures and the Dominion says so. Again I ask the question,

does any hon. gentleman want to debate the right of this parliament to interfere with local autonomy?-to interfere with the city of Toronto's waterworks, or the city of Toronto's electric light system, or the city of Toronto's police force, and the like? Nobody does, and if he did he would have no regard for his own reputation. It is inconceivable.
What is the other question? We learn that, under the agreement of confederation, property and civil rights are matters which are left to the provinces. Well, I wonder how many people think that the Dominion knows better than the provinces what ought to be done with property and civil rights. I wonder how many provinces would feel like handing over the control of their property and civil rights to the Dominion, or, conversely, how many people in the Dominion think the federal authority ought to try to wrest those rights from the provinces? The whole truth of the matter, Mr. Speaker, is that Canada's difficulties are not constitutional, they are functional. It is not so much the structure, it is what we are doing with the structure, that is making trouble to-day in Canada-nothing else. Suppose we were to be asked to correct the troubles of Canada, how would we go about it? How would we characterize it? I think we would say, in the first place, lack of employment. I think we would say, in the second instance, the loss that comes from lessened employment, the diminished pay rolls and purchasing power. I think we would say, in the third instance, lack of population. I think we would say, in the fourth instance, the exodus to the United States. And I think we would say finally, burdensome taxation. Mr. Speaker, in the name of common sense what constitutional difficulties arise by reason of these troubles?-which I think will be generally admitted to be the chief troubles in the country. What constitutional difficulties confront us in connection with their consideration? None, absolutely none. All that is necessaiy to do is to put the question in order to elicit that response. That is not the trouble. We have got any amount of constitutional power to deal with all these questions, with all the questions which are due to our troubles to-day. No, it is not a question of law, it is not a constitutional question, it is a functional disease which afflicts this country very badly at the present time. In other words our constitution enables us to function, and if we are not functioning it is our own fault and not the fault of the constitution.
Now, suppose we go to the third point- I have no desire to speak at undue length- and that is that the general feeling in Can-

B.N.A. Act Amendment
ada to-day is one of perfect willingness to still continue to form an important-and as I said before an ever increasingly important- part of the British Empire, There ought to be no room for doubt as to that. I admit that we have a lot of dialecticians who go up and down the country cleverly arguing that black is white, and never content until they have proved it to their own satisfaction. I admit that, but I am also equally positive in affirming that the Canadian people want no such changes, they want to carry on business as they are carrying on business now, they want a fair chance of considering on their merits the real troubles, functional as they are, of this country, without constitutional and other difficulties being constantly drawn over the track. We know that the heart of Canad'a beats as strongly and as truly as it did in 1914. But there is the stranger that is without the gates, there is the man who does not know, there is the man who holds every ill-considered word, every effort to get something for nothing, as an evidence of the dismemberment of the British Empire. All you have got to do to see that is simply to read' the papers. I have heard some gentlemen say-not in this House I gladly admit- that it ill became the Canadian people to form part of a warlike empire like the British Empire. Mr. Speaker, can you imagine greater nonsense? I wish some of the gentlemen who talk that way would take the trouble to go over to the good old Mother Country, bleeding herself white, as she is, in order to honestly and fairly discharge her obligations to society-to society, yes, ana' to her own people,-to discharge her obligations to her own people as well as her international obligations. I should like them to go over there and consider exactly the plight the grand old country is in. Why, if there is a country in the world that is interested in peace, that is interested in commerce, it is Great Britain, Every man knows it. What is the reason of her position to-day? What is the reason there are 1,200,000 unemployed' men walking the streets of Britain supported by her ratepayers and a burden on her diminished commerce? Every thoughtful mind knows it. We know very well that we could have issues on fiscal policy, but over and above fiscal policy, there is the fact that of all the nations in the world the Mother Country is the great trading countiy, she traa'es in every quarter of the globe, and her markets as a result of the war are such that, workshop of the world as she has been called, she can scarcely function any longer with efficiency. I happened to be in England this year, and one thing that a man, no matter
how suspicious his mind might be, could not find there was anybody who wanted war, or further expeditions, or further incursions, or further risks.
No, no. The whole truth is simply this: that by taking our share and our part, I hope some day we will be able to so run things in this country, so adjust our financial affairs that we shall be in a position to play a worthy part; but I think the best thing for Canada to-day, not only for herself but for a world sadly rent by war, is to stay just where she is within the boundaries of the one great vehicle through which peace to-day can be ensured, the British Empire.

My right hon.
friend I am afraid does not want to get the point. I agree that there is none. I have been saying that there is none, but I do say that anything and everything which goes in the slightest degree to throw any question upon what I believe to be the absolute fundamental truth is bad all round, bad for both of our mother countries, and this country in particular. If England needs peace, France certainly needs peace; and to-day if there is one thing which is a nightmare in France it is the thought of the return of the Germans, and if there is one thing that gives a fair chance, a fair hope, of a solution of the whole difficulty, it is the co-operation of France and Great Britain. And if we do everything we can to assure the outside world that we are with those great countries to the fullest extent, that we, as part and parcel of the British Empire desire to see that everything is done w'hich would bring pacification so earnestly desired by both of those great countries, then we are playing the best part we can play. And in playing that part any suggestion that there is any desire to in any 'way weaken our ties with the Mother Country, with the empire, works harm to the general good, to Canada, to France, to Great Britain and the empire itself.
Let us recapitulate. Let us understand that none of these troubles are troubles which should be held against either the Mother Country on the one hand or the British Empire itself: that all our constitution difficulties, our difficulties of the moment, are difficulties of our own making; that all the troubles that give rise to these difficulties are the infringement of rights, either provincial or Dominion; and that Canada absolutely and fully is mistress within her own house.

less difficulties, it does not make them less real; and I do sincerely hope we may avoid any possibility of friction and danger arising out of a too rigid constitution by taking the suggestion which was made yesterday by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) and submitting this whole question to this conference which is to be called, in order that they may fully and frankly discuss it. I am satisfied that whatever may be the views of the hon. member for West York (Sir Henry Drayton) there is a feeling in Canada fairly widely prevalent that the situation at the present time is not satisfactory, that some modification ought to be made, and I am only going to throw out this suggestion. If, for instance, the reformation, the modification, or the abolition, of the Senate is under consideration in this country, and our constitution binds us so that one province can absolutely tie up the whole matter and prevent action for all time to come, we are face to face with a very serious practical difficulty and will have to meet it. The confederation pact or constitution may be a treaty. We shall have to observe our obligations. But it occurs to me that treaties need modification from time to time as conditions change. I have in my mind a little matter that some year or two ago gave considerable trouble to the government, namely the dispute arising between the Six Nations Indians in my own constituency and the Dominion as to the jurisdiction of Canada in that reserve. The Indians claimed that they were a separate nation, guaranteed all solemn rights by the Haldimand treaty. Although that might be so, a literal application of that contention would reduce us to such absurdities of practice that nobody in his senses would refuse to admit the need of modification. I do plead with the House with the member for St Hyacinthe-Rouville (Mr. Morin) who spoke so well yesterday on this question, that we ought to face the situation from the present point of view, and perhaps there is no better way than that suggested by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe). I do trust, that the matter will not be overlooked and that the conference may not sit and ignore this really important feature.

In

the opinions of the representatives of all those provinces which now form part of the Dominion could be collected and fully considered. The hon member for South York (Mr. Maclean) has suggested that this parliament should be empowered to amend our constitution. I do not believe that it was ever the intention of the Fathers of Confederation to give to this parliament power to change the basis of confederation, and it would be a radical amendment to give to this parliament such power. I do not believe, either, that this parliament, after obtaining powers from the various provinces, should be able to suggest an amendment to confederation. On the contrary, I would suggest that if any amendments are to be proposed, the best way is that suggested ;d the Speech from the Throne, by convening a conference from all sections of Canada and letting all those who will be convened there fully discuss the proposed amendments, consider the pros and cons, and come to a concrete and definite proposition.
It is very curious to read in the newspapers, as is suggested by the hon. member for West York (Sir Henry Drayton), that there is a state of unrest in Canada and that to remedy it we should amend the constitution.

I hear some aspirants who

It is, perhaps, advisable that the period of tenure of office be not the same as that of members of the House of Commons. This is the case in many other countries, and we can take, with advantage, a lesson from the constitutions of some other countries. Consider, for instance, the constitution of France, where the Senate is elected for a period of nine years, renewable by thirds every three years. That will furnish the safety-valve, the degree of guarantee that at a given moment parliament will not be stampeded by a current of opinion. Apart from that, however, I do not believe that the laws of a democratic country should be passed by one of the Houses of Parliament which is not responsible to the people of Canada; but the best way to obtain that amendment is, as I say, that suggested in the Speech from the Throne, by convening a conference of all those who were a party to the pact of confederation and getting their opinions, so that the objections, if any, might be heard.
I, for one, would like to see some changes in our constitution. Some years ago, after the Treaty of Versailles, I heard in this House some hon. gentlemen then sitting on the treasury benches, for instance, Right Hon. Mr. Doherty and other members of the former administration, contending that Canada was a nation; that a dazzling light had been shed on this country showing her forth to the nations of the world a nation equal to all the others. These were fine words, and if they were not absolutely true, they expressed, I think, the ardent desire of all true Canadians who are proud to come out of the period of infancy, who want to become of age and to exercise all the powers that rest with a man and citizen. But these words, that Canada is a nation, do not mean, nor do I believe that any important section of public opinion in Canada holds them to mean, secession from the British Empire. So that when we hear the hon. member for West York (Sir Henry Drayton) saying that there are important sections of the Canadian people who sincerely desire secession from the British Empire, I think the hon. gentleman is mistaken.

speechtext: I understood him to say so. At any rate, I am glad if the hon. member believes as I do, that no important section of public opinion in Canada desires to see anything of this kind. But if we are a nation, if, to use the words of a former Minister of Justice, a dazzling light has been shed on this country showing her forth as a nation equal to all others among the nations of the world, then it seems to me that some amendments to our constitution should be brought about so that the facts may be made to agree with the assertions. What other nation under the sun is there, independent, equal to all others, which has to send in last resort its appeal to the tribunal of any other country? Which one, among all the other independent nations of the world, is obliged to pass through the machinery of some ambassador of a different country in order to be accredited to foreign powers? Which among the independent nations of the world is obliged to receive as its chief magistrate a man appointed at the suggestion of an authority which is not within the country itself? I say, therefore, that if we are really a nation, as I hope we shall become, and always within the British Commonwealth, I should like to see the Governor General of Canada appointed, not on the advice of the British ministry but on the advice of the Canadian ministers to His Majesty the King.

4 p.m. adian statesman. He wished to have an interview with the President of the French republic and for this purpose he went to the office of the Canadian High Commissioner in Paris. The High Commissioner could not arrange the interview, however. Why? Simply because the Canadian High Commissioner in Paris is not accredited to the President of the French republic. This gentleman had to go to the British embassy and there request the British ambassador to arrange the meeting with the President of the French republic. Yet any citizen of the small principality of Monaco can go to the minister of that country in Paris and without any other formality have a similar meeting arranged. I do not contend that it is a matter of capital importance, but I do think that it is a matter of national dignity; and' it seems to me that our high commissioners abroad, in England. France and other countries, should have the same standing as the diplomatic ministers who represent Roumania, Greece, Belgium and other nations that are hardly of any greater importance to-day than Canada.
As regard appeals to the Privy Council, it may be in our interest to remain in the present situation in respect of appeals on constitutional matters as well as in respect of appeals of grace to His Majesty. The Privy Council advise His Majesty the King on certain questions, particularly in appeals of grace; and in matters of this kind it might be well for us to remain as we are. But I fail to see why we should uselessly multiply appeals in matters of civil rights and of local interest. Why should we multiply uselessly these appeals and ask a few gentlemen sitting in London, for whom I have the greatest respect, finally to dispose of questions of this character affecting civil rights, commercial rights and other affairs of that kind within the province of our own parliament and legislatures to pass upon?

It is one of the privileges of the crown of England to grant an appeal to the Privy Council when it chooses to do so, even when such appeal does not lie a-s of right. My right hon. friend must know that,
I am sure. And besides, there is the appeal of grace in criminal matters, in which His Majesty can always exercise that prerogative of pardon which everyone recognizes as inherent in the British crown. So that as regards the exercise of the prerogatives of the crown, I would by no means try to curtail them. Of course my right hon. friend knows that this grace is exercised on the advice of the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council, who advise His Majesty in respect of them. So far as that is concerned I would maintain the appeal. I would maintain it also in matters which have reference to our constitutional rights. The tribunal in London may be more independent and more apt to render justice when questions arise with regard to the respective rights of the Dominion or of the provinces. In respect to that, some have quoted the example of the highest tribunals of France and of the United States, and we have pointed out that in those countries even constitutional questions are determined 'by the highest court in the land. On these three points, therefore, I think we might well correct our constitution with a view to having the Canadian nation conform in this respect to the status, which, it has been urged, she attained following the treaty of Versailles and the various other treaties which were signed thereafter. I do not believe we can fairly boast of being a nation equal to all others until some such changes as these take place; until then we are not equal to the other nations of the world. As to the method of bringing about any such amendment, I fully agree with that set forth in the Speech from the Throne and explained yesterday by the hon. Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) as the only method by which we should proceed in any attempt to give all sections of the Canadian people who entered into the confederation pact of 1867 the right to amend it. As in the case of a contract between private individuals, you cannot change the British North America Act without first convening a conference similar to that as the result of which the act originally came into being.

I am unable to see that our freedom is in any way restricted under the present conditions. If my hon. friend does not want Canada to become an independent nation so that we can send our own ambassadors to Paris, as has been suggested, at enormous cost to this country-a cost which is at present met out of the imperial exchequer, affording a service which is just as good as that which could be given by any person we would send-if he does not want Canada to be independent, why bother about this pro-
posed change? Up to the present time the British North America Act has answered very well in this country. I cannot recall any attack that has been made upon it as insufficient to meet the needs of Canada. We must remember that this was an act that the Imperial government passed in order to establish harmony in this Dominion. We had three different groups in Canada, all under different governments, and by this time we would have had four or perhaps five had the confederation not taken place. The British North America Act was passed to harmonize the groups that then existed and to start Canada on its way to nationhood within the empire. I submit that it has accomplished that purpose, and accomplished it better, perhaps, than any instrument that can be cited as a parallel in any part of the world. That being the case, why should we now begin an agitation to destroy the existing conditions and introduce something which in my judgment would be a greater cause of friction and inharmony in Canada than the British North America Act? If we want our constitution amended at any time we can have that done. We have had the act amended every time we have asked for it, and we can have it amended again in any particular at any time we ask for it. We are not tied down by some ironclad agreement that cannot be amended if the country as a whole desire to amend it. And if we had this new constitution it would not be right to amend it by the bare majority as my hon. friend suggests. That certainly would not lead to the continuance of harmony and good feeling throughout this country. I object on principle to the proposal of the resolution that these two houses of parliament can at any time amend our constitution by a majority. I think that;would be a dangerous thing to do. We must remember that we have in the Maritime provinces, in the western provinces, and in Quebec and Ontario, views that are widely divergent, and if by reason of a preponderance of members from one particular section, say the west, the constitution could be amended to the disadvantage of the Maritime provinces, as the people of those provinces might consider, then we would have a state of friction in this country that would be dangerous and that might lead to something a great deal worse than anything that is possible under present conditions. In the United States they can amend their constitution only if two-thirds of the states by a two-thirds majority agree to it. The most substantial safeguards are provided there against amending their constitution. There should also be safeguards in this country, and the

B.N.A. Act Amendment
very best safeguard we can. get is to make it requisite for this country to go to the imperial authorities under whom we live and move and have our being as a nation, and let them act as arbitrators in whatever it is desired to do ic Canada in the way of changing our constitution. Give Canada the right to change its constitution by a majority of these two houses of parliament, as my hon. friend proposes, and limit that as you will, provide as does this resolution that parliament would have no power to affect the rights of minorities, put that limitation in to-day, and there is no certainty, there can be no certainty, that that would be the limitation of the future. Give Canada the right to amend its constitution partially, and Canada will soon demand the right to amend its constitution wholly.

I believe that Canada can make greater contributions to civilization as a part of the empire than under any other status. All hon. members will admit that the British Empire has made-I was going to say the greatest-contributions to civilization of any nation, but perhaps I ought to be considerate of some of my hon. friends opposite who have another mother country, and say that her contributions have been enormous. She has given free institutions to the world'. She has developed them, and they have been copied by practically every other country. I am of the opinion that here in Canada we will in time by the admixture of the English, Irish, Scottish, French, and other blood develop a race of men that will be just a little superior to the race of the Old Land, and that as a result of our growth, individually and as a

nation, we will be able to aid in the development of a higher civilization to a greater degree than even the Mother Country has done. The Canadian breed has shown what it is capable of d'oing in the war, and the Canadian people in civil life have never given a greater demonstration of their endurance under difficult conditions than they are doing to-day. So that whether it is in war or in civil life Canadians have the right to hold up their heads as among the most enduring, the most intelligent and, I think perhaps, the most capable of the nations of the world. We cannot be regarded in the light of slaves, or serfs, or anything of that kind; Canadians demonstrated that in 1837.

In reply to his question I have nothing more to say than that. Returning to my subject let me say that I believe Canada has more to gain, and that the empire has more to gain, by Can-ad'a's continuance in that empire, rather than by a change in a contrary direction. Our continuance in it, year by year and with every decade that passes, will strengthen that empire, and I do not see any reason why we should turn now and take the first step in the direction of independence unless we are suffering from difficulties that cannot be remedied otherwise.

Mr. Speaker, the question which we are discussing is one of the most important, that could be brought before us. We could discuss tariffs, we could discuss financial matters, we could discuss estimates and the ordinary bills that come before this House and still remain within the realm of matters that are purely domestic, matters which by common consent can be changed as soon as the will of the parliament is made apparent to that end. But the question that was raised by the hon. member for South York (Mr. Maclean) in the motion before us touches the very life of the nation, it goes to the very core of our national being,

B.NA. Act Amendment
and for that reason it is a question of first importance.
I must confess that in listening to my hon. friend from West Toronto (Mr. Hocken) and to my hon. friend from West York (Sir Henry Drayton) I felt that they must have been very much in the realm of dreamland during the last ten years.

The fact is that Canada
has moved forward tremendously in the last fifty years. Those of us who have read history know the circumstances in Canada that brought about the confederation of the then existing provinces. I quite agree with the argument advanced by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) yesterday that the confederation pact was in the nature of a treaty. It was the result of different provinces getting together and agreeing upon a solution that would lead them out of their difficulties. But while that was one of the reasons behind the confederation understanding or agreement in 1867, there was also another aspiration behind it, and it was voiced, perhaps most strongly, by the great architect of confederation, Sir John A. Macdonald, for in large measure he was the architect of confederation, even if he could not claim credit for originating the idea. And what was that aspiration? At that time we had on the northern part of the North American continent several distinct governments-crown colonies if you like, crown colonies, I mean, in the sense that while they enjoyed in very considerable measure the right of governing themselves, they were, so far as their relations with each other were concerned, completely isolated. And one of the most important, one of the strongest ideas behind the whole conception of confederation was that these several provinces might be united in one whole and form a nucleus for a nation on the northern half of North America. That hope is set out frequently in the confederation debates: and the notion that Sir John Macdonald had, the notion that the other Fathers of Confederation had, that they were laying the foundation for the establishment of a nation, a free nation, in North America, has simply been carried forward from that time until this. And we have made great advances Mr. Speaker, as I hope I shall presently show, in the fifty-six years that have elapsed since confederation.
Now what are the advances that we have made? In the first place let me say that these
advances have come mainly, though not altogether by any means, within the last ten years, since the outbreak of the Great War in 1914. First, we raised an army, an immense army. We sent that army overseas, and it fought under the direction and under the control of the Canadian parliament. It was known as the Canadian army. It was not thrown in as part of the British army, nor was it recognized as part of the British army throughout the whole war. The second thing of even greater import that occurred was the fact that Canada claimed the right-

Is there anyone in his senses who would assert that that was in contemplation at the time confederation was achieved? There is nothing on the record, so far as I have been able to find out, that would support that view.
We have made further progress. In 1919, as a result of negotiations between Sir Robert Borden, who was then Prime Minister of Canada, and the British government-and it is well known the question was taken up at that time with the United States-Canada secured the right to send to the United States an ambassador who would handle all matters affecting Canada at the capital of our great neighbour to the south. I ask again, was that contemplated when the confederation pact was established in 1867? Another step forward has been taken since then, when my hon. friend the Minister of Justice, clothed with power from His Majesty, went to Washington and negotiated with the United States a treaty covering the halibut fisheries on the Pacific ocean,-a treaty that has since been ratified by both this parliament and the United

States, and which binds only these two countries. That is another evidence of progress in the matter of nationhood. All the evidence, Mr. Speaker, goes to prove beyond any question of doubt that we have advanced beyond the state we were in in 1867, when the four provinces with organized governments in what is now part of the territory of this Dominion were brought together.
When I come to the resolution of the hon. member for South York (Mr. Maclean) I say at once that I agree, wholly with the purpose he has in mind. I think this country has risen to the state and the dignity, not only in the estimation of the people of Canada, but in her relations with the outside world, where we should have the right under certain conditions which I shall presently mention, of fixing and determining our own constitution. I do not agree with the method my hon. friend suggests. I do not think for a moment that it would be wise-and in this I quite agree with the objections raised by my hon. friend from West Toronto (Mr. Hocken)- to leave the question of amending our constitution to an open vote in this House or in the other branch of this parliament.

My hon. friend the Minister of Justice yesterday argued that confederation was in the nature of a treaty, and I agree with him in that assertion. That- being the case, his suggestion that the matter be approached through the avenue of a conference with all the provinces is the first step that should be taken in dealing with it. It is quite clear that in any consideration of this matter we must be governed by the circumstances of our situation. I can quite appreciate the anxiety, or, shall I say, even the fear, that my hon. friends from the province of Quebec may entertain as to the position which that province would be in in respect of the peculiar rights it enjoys under the constitution today, were we placed in the situation in this country where the constitution could be amended by the ordinary means of majority rule. Consequently I wish to state very

clearly upon that matter that, in my humble opinion, the safeguards that our French Canadian fellow-citizens enjoy to-day under the federation arrangement should abso'utely and irrevocably be provided for and maintained. There is no fair-minded person in the whole Dominion of Canada, I am convinced, who would wish for a single moment to deny them that right. I am convinced that a way can be found whereby the rights enjoyed by our French Canadian citizens which they naturally hold very dearly, can be safeguarded and the fullest protection given to them in that regard. We frequently ask ourselves the question- and, Mr. Speaker, let me point out that not only do Canadians ask themselves the question, but other countries are also commencing to ask the question-is Canada a nation? And notwithstanding the eloquent speeches delivered by my hon. friend for West Toronto and my hon. friend for West York we cannot escape giving an answer to that question. I dissent wholly from the view expressed by my hon. friend for West York and the view expressed by the hon. member for West Toronto that any suggestion that Canada be given the power to amend her own constitution is evidence of disloyalty to the Motherland. Sir, I resent that argument.

There is just one other
point that I wish to make, as I do not desire to participate now at any length in the debate, as a matter of fact, I had scarcely expected to take part in it, but I could not sit in my seat and listen to the arguments of the hon. member for West Toronto without challenging them. What are we in Canada? We are all good Canadians who want to see this country prosper. We realize the economic and financial difficulties which the country is passing through. We realize the difficulties in government, in maintaining a national unity, that arise from our geographical conditions and also from the-shall I say? -mixed character of our population. We have the great province of Quebec, with its three million Freneh-Canadians, as loyal and fine a class of citizens as we have in the Dominion. We have the citizens of Canada of Anglo-Saxon origin. We have, in addition to that, hundreds of thousands of citizens, people who have come to this country from alien lands to make their homes here, to grow up and develop as Canadians. What is the thing that will best draw all these elements together? Is it not some pride in a national spirit, some conception of a national entity? speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have had occasion to give some little thought and study to this particular question and that is why I participate in this debate this afternoon. The question is an extremely complicated one, and any member of this House who has taken the trouble to study the constitution and development of Canada and of Great Britain must realize the difficulties encountered in an effort to pass a resolution of this kind which embodies the terms of an amendment which it is sought that the Imperial House should pass concerning our constitution. When confederation was brought about, three important resolutions were passed at the Quebec conference in 1865. They are of sufficient importance and so fundamental to our constitution that I propose to read them, particularly as they are short. They state, with reference to the North American provinces:
1.	The system of government best adapted under existing circumstances to protect the diversified interests of the several provinces, and secure harmony and permanency in the working of the union, would be a general government charged with matters of common interest to the whole country, and local governments for each of the Canadas, and for the provinces of Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island, charged with the control of local matters in their respective sections.
2.	In framing a constitution for the general government, the conference, with a view to the perpetuation of our connection with the Mother Country, and the promotion of the best interests of the people of these provinces, desire to follow the model of the British constitution so far as our circumstances permit.
3.	The executive authority or government shall be vested in the sovereign of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland, and be administered according to the well-understood principles of the British constitution, by a sovereign personally, or by the representative of the sovereign duly authorized.
There is one feature of this debate which I do not think has been emphasized and it is vital to the consideration of the resolution before the House. The hon. member for Brant (Mr. Good) touched on it lightly. Our constitution involves mot only the British North America Act, which is the written or fixed or inflexible portion of our constitution, but the unwritten part of our constitution. In other words, our constitution comprises the

written portion, which is the British North America Act and which is specific, and the unwritten portion, which we find in such institutions as the cabinet. In the government and constitution of this country, we have in practice precedents, conventions and understandings that you will not find anywhere in the British North America Act. Take, for example, the institution of the cabinet. You will not find that word written anywhere in our constitution. You will not find the word "cabinet" in the British constitution, yet it is the governing and controlling factor in the government of this countiy. Supposing, for example, that there was an adverse vote in the House, what would follow? There is no law to oblige the government to resign, but the precedents and understandings of our constitution make it necessary. But if the government in the face of such adverse vote was refused supply and still endeavoured to enforce by act of parliament the collection of taxes, the courts of the land would be available to enable our citizens to refuse to comply with such an attempt.
The cabinet is the central pivot of responsible government.. It dates back in Great Britain to the time of Charles I. Before then the cabinet had been responsible to the king but through the efforts of the Cabal of that day the responsibility was shifted, and the ministry was made answerable to parliament. Some may not know that in Canada cabinet responsibility to the legislative institutions of the country did not become a fact until 1842. Prior to that date the cabinet was responsible to the Governor General. So that in the course of the constitutional development of this country there have become embodied in the constitution fictions, conventions, precedents and understandings which have all had a practical part in the government of the country. Now the resolution which is before the House proposes to alter the written portion of the constitution, that portion which has been enacted by the Imperial parliament. And as one speaker after another has indicated, that enactment did not originate with the Imperial government, it was not something super-imposed upon this country, but was an understanding or agreement arrived at between the component parts of the British North American provinces which entered into confederation. This fact is clearly expressed in the preamble to the act:
Whereas the provinces of Canada, Nova Scotia and New Brunswick have expressed their desire to be federally united into one Dominion under the crown of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland, with a constitution similar in principle to that of the United Kingdom.

B.N.A. Act Amendment
In that principle you have the unwritten portion of the British constitution, the flexible portion which proves so practical and useful in every dominion wherein it can be adapted to the peculiarities of race and people concerned. And the fourth paragraph reads:
And -whereas it is expedient that provision be made for the eventual admission into the union of other parts of British North America-
You have, therefore, in this paragraph a very clear statement or understanding of the situation and we cannot as a Canadian parliament change our constitution and pass legislation of the kind proposed, even with the suggested amendment, which provides for the consent first of all the provinces. I submit that the complications are too numerous and the problem is too wide for us to undertake anything of the kind at this time. I am sure that hon. mem'bers must be fully sensitive to their duty and responsibility to precipitate an ill-considered debate on this subject at this juncture. The present discussion will be reviewed from one end of the empire to the other, and it would be distinctly unwise for us to jump to any hasty conclusion in dealing with this question. I think we would be rash in approving a resolution which is uncertain in its terms and indefinite in its meaning. I would ask the House to refer to the resolution for a moment. It provides:
The parliament of the Dominion upon first obtaining the consent of the provinces may amend the said British North America Act when it may see fit to do so, but it is not empowered to pass any amendment affecting the rights guaranteed in said act to minorities.
Does this mean that every specific amendment would have first of all to be approved by the provinces and then submitted to this parliament? Or does it mean that a general power of amendment would first have to be approved by the provinces before being submitted to parliament? Some hon. members nod their heads to the second proposition. But the question is, which is the true interpretation of this proposed bill which seeks to change the constitution under which we have been operating since 1867? Which is the true proposal? I submit that as soon as you undertake to place before the provinces of Canada a proposed amendment such as is set out in this resolution you will create endless confusion. I am convinced that interminable discussions would arise which would prove adverse to our interests. There would be speculative debates on theories of our international relationships and the relationships of this country with the Mother Country, to say nothing of a number of other problems which would follow in consequence. At this 21
time when the nations of the world are suffering economic distress, when there are grave troubles in Europe and elsewhere, when Canada itself is faced with a great national debt, a huge railway problem, and' economic difficulties of a severe nature, it would be exceedingly unwise to open a question of this kind, especially since it has not been shown in one single statement that there is any 5 p.m. demand for the action which the resolution proposes, or anything to warrant such a change.
When we broach the question of amending our constitution by changing it only in part, that is to say, the written portion of it, we are at once in the realm of international relationships; not only is our relationship with Great Britain involved but our international relationships are also brought to the forefront. There has been a gradual development of our position in that respect, and I would commend to the attention of the House a little book of Sir Robert Borden's entitled Canadian Constitutional Studies. From that book it will be seen that in 1917-18 Canada in fact obtained the recognition of the principle of nationhood and complete autonomy in the empire. I quote the following from page 111:
During 1917 and 1918, the Imperial War conference also proceeded with its deliberations. Its most important discussion in 1917 was concerned with the question of future constitutional relations and resulted in the following resolution:
" The Imperial War conference are of opinion that the readjustment of the constitutional relations of the component parts of the empire is too important and intricate a subject to be dealt with during the war, [DOT]and that it should form the subject of a special Imperial conference to be summoned as soon as possible after the cessation of hostilities.
" They deem it their duty, however, to place on record their view that any such readjustment, while thoroughly preserving all existing powers of self-government and complete control of domestic affairs, should be based upon a full recognition of the dominions as autonomous nations of an Imperial commonwealth and of India as an important portion of the same, should recognize the right of the dominions and India to an adequate voice in foreign policy and in foreign relations, and should provide effective arrangements for continuous consultation in all important matters of common Imperial concern, and for such necessary concerted action, founded on consultation, as the several governments may determine."
I propose to read a few of these sections because they are the words of a great authority on the subject and have a bearing on the resolution in question.
This resolution establishes the basis of future cooperation; it gives clear recognition to equality of nationhood between the dominions and the Mother Country; and it marks one of the most important, and possibly one of the final stages in the evolution of constitutional relations within the British commonwealth. In 1921 the same principle was re-asserted. Lord Milner, speaking on this important matter in

B.N.A. Act Amendment

1920 (before the representatives of the overseas dominions, emphasized the same view in these words:
" The only possibility of a continuance of the British Empire is on a basis of absolute out-and-out equal partnership between the United Kingdom and the dominions. I say that without any kind of reservation whatsoever. It is very easy to say that; but undoubtedly the working out of it in practice without bringing about the severance of relations between us and the dominions will be one of the most complicated tasks which statesmanship has ever had to face. I am not afraid of it, and yet I have to admit that the difficulties are such that our best efforts may end in failure. I hope not. At any rate, there is no other way out.
At a later stage the powers of the Dominion with respect to treaty making had developed, and I again quote the words of Sir Robert Borden, which summarize the situation very nicely:
A further development relates to the signature and ratification of the various treaties concluded at the conference. In view of the new position secured, and of the part played by the dominion representatives at the peace table, it was considered that the treaty should be signed by dominion plenipotentiaries, and should be submitted for approval to the dominion parliaments. Accordingly the Prime Minister of Canada proposed that the assent of the King as high contracting party to the various treaties should, in respect of the dominions, be expressed by the signature of dominion plenipotentiaries, and that the preamble and other formal parts of the treaties should be drafted accordingly.
The treaty making power of the Dominion is not a new one. Then we gained a new position in the League of Nations. Sir Robert Borden says:
The new status of the Dominion is manifested again in the constitution of the League of Nations. Having gained at the Peace conference the position of " powers with special interests" the dominions took the ground that they should be similarly accepted in the future international relationships contemplated by the league. The League of Nations Commission, while inclined to admit this position in principle, did not at the outset accept all its implications. ... In its final form, as amended and incorporated in the treaty of Peace with Germany, the covenant fully recognizes the status of the dominions.
Now, I want to draw the attention of the House to another point which is interwoven with this question of amending our constitution. As soon as you enter upon the programme of changing the British North America Act, apart altogether from the relationship of one province with the other you have the great question of Canada's relationship to foreign countries and a nurhber of other far-reaching problems which should also be considered. I suggest to hon. members that before giving their approval to the resolution that has been proposed or the principle which it involves they should consider this matter in the light of the conditions which confront the country and from the practical point of view.
What is to be gained by passing a resolution of this kind? There are no practical

questions out of which this proposal has arisen. All that can result is discussion and controversy from one end of Canada to the other on the question of loyalty to Canada's relationship to the empire and things of that kind. Here we are assembled with extremely grave and important questions of a practical nature confronting us. I referred to them a moment ago-our taxation, our railways, our economic difficulties, the tariff, if you will, and so on. What is to be gained by this resolution, beyond some political effect in some parts of Canada, an effect which may carry with it the arousing of feelings of prejudice and the expression of likes or dislikes in different sections of the country?
I believe this resolution should be refused by the House. If the government are serious in announcing their intention to bring down legislation calling upon the provinces to consider the matter of the amendment of our constitution; if it is not merely a political intention, then when they bring down that legislation I hope they will be able to submit something of a substantial character in the way of a demand from some section of the country for such a change in our constitution as is proposed. For my part I cannot but believe that the problem is fraught with too grave difficulties. The history of the development of our constitution is such that the man of business should hesitate at this juncture, having regard to the conditions in the world generally. I heard Mr. Ewart give a most interesting discussion of conditions among the countries of Europe and an outline of how the nations of the world had been chopped up as a result of the war, how the elements of conflagration exist in many parts of Europe. With all these national and international questions of a practical nature awaiting solution, why should this House occupy its time in the discussion of such a resolution as my hon. friend proposes?

Mr. Speaker, the question before the House in undoubtedly one of very great interest. Though I have given it some consideration and have some opinions upon it, I refrain from giving those opinions now for the simple reason that I have been assured, and I think rightly, that this parliament has no power to do what I or anybody else might think it well to do in regard to our constitution. We have been assured by the authorities on constitutional law-and I think this is the attitude they take so far as they have spoken in this House -that the British North America Act is a sacred compact and that it cannot be altered

B.N.A. Act Amendment
by this parliament alone; that if an alteration is to be made all the parties to the pact must first be consulted and their consent to the change obtained.
In the Speech from the Throne there is an announcement that a conference is to be held at which representatives of all the different parties to the compact known as the British North America Act are to meet. It has been suggested by the hon. Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) that the issue involved in this resolution would be a proper question for that conference to consider. In view, therefore, of these considerations, I move, seconded by the hon. member for West Edmonton (Mr. Kennedy):
That the following words be inserted after the word " minorities " in the second .paragraph of the resolution: " and that, before further action be taken on the proposed resolution, the same be referred to the conference proposed in the Speech from the Throne for consideration and recommendation.''
