Mr. Speaker, at the commencement of this discussion I had no intention of taking part in it, but several matters have come up in the course of the remarks of hon. members, particularly as regards the province of Quebec, and it seems to me that one should have these matters well in mind before even suggesting that the resolution now before the House should be submitted to a conference as is proposed.
It seems to me that those who have discussed this resolution particularly some hon. members from this side of the House, have utterly failed to remember what were the circumstances of history and what were the facts which led up to the British North America Act of 1867. While perhaps many hon. members in this House may recall to mind those facts, I do not think it would be very much amiss if I, in the very few minutes I propose to take part in this discussion, should ask particularly those gentlemen from the province of Quebec to bear those facts in mind, because they are very salient indeed, and are very germane to this resolution we are discussing to-day, indeed, very germane to any question of conferences which might take place in the future apropos of any amendments to the British North America Act.
What are those historical facts leading up to the enactment of the British North America Act? Our first constitution in this country was the Quebec Act of 1774; I am speaking from memory as regards dates. That act took in, as I am very well aware, a great stretch of country running westward almost to the Missouri river. The limits of that
21i
country were changed by the treaty of Versailles in 1783, which made the westerly limits of what was then the province of Quebec the Great Lakes. After that we come down to the Constitutional Act of 1791, which divided the two provinces of Canada into Upper and Lower Canada. That act ran its course. Various matters came up in the administration of this country, ideas were engendered between the two races, and the culmination of this act of 1791 was the fight for responsible government in 1837. That was the result of the Constitutional Act of 1791.
Then we come down to the Act of Union in 1841, which brought the provinces of Upper and Lower Canada into one province, as the result of the Durham report. There again we found all kinds of difficulties brought up and ideas engendered between the races, ideas of religion, ideas of representation by population, and half a hundred other questions, until finally responsible government absolutely broke down. The suspicions engendered between the provinces and between the races under the Act of Union of 1841 were such as to render it utterly impossible for this country to proceed in any normal sense of the word with government at all. Out of all those difficulties that took place issued the Quebec resolutions. Those same difficulties took place in the Maritimes also. There also they decided they wanted a union, and the conference at Charlottetown took place, to which conference certain delegates went from Canada, and those delegates subsequently joined together at the Quebec conference, and it was from the Quebec conference that the Act of Confederation of 1867 was brought about,
Coming as I do from the province of Quebec I would like my hon. friends from that province to bear in mind these historical facts which brought about our Confederation Act. I would like them to bear in mind also the various difficulties and the various safeguards that were provided as regards our own province of Quebec. That is an extremely important matter for them to remember. I am of the province of Quebec. I live there with my French-Canadian compatriots in peace and harmony, and I say this; there is nothing so far as I can see in the British North America Act that can be changed to assist us in the very least in the province of Quebec in particular, to say nothing of the rest of Canada.
I listened with a great deal of pleasure this afternoon to the speech of my hon. friend from Marquette (Mr. Crerar). He stated' among other matters that we should have the right to fix our own constitution. I assume he meant by that the fixing of our
B.N.A. Act Amendment

constitution for interior matters only; he could have meant nothing else at all. We cannot fix our constitution for exterior matters in any respect, but as regards exterior matters I will speak in a moment. I would ask in what way, and with what advantage, can we change the act at present in force? Where will any province be assisted? You can imagine how a province might be injured in many ways. You can well imagine in the event of a conference taking place, and in the event of various opinions coming forth at that conference, that matters might happen in such a way as to reopen very many of these selfsame questions that came up at the Quebec conference, and which were settled by compromise at the Quebec conference itself, and as a result of which the British North America Act came forth. I repeat, what advantage is to be gained by any province by trying to give ourselves here in this parliament the right to change the act which was the result of compromises of a most severe nature, compromises which were the result also of events which took place and which led up to that conference, events of a most serious and foretelling nature.
My hon. friend from Marquette in his very masterly way also said that it was vital for the development of this nation that we should have the power to amend our constitution. I fail to see how this nation can be developed in the slightest degree by amending from the interior our own constitution. As a matter of fact, this nation was built up under that very constitution. That constitution has been the very cornerstone of all the rights of the various provinces within the nation. Nothing can be added to the rights of the provinces by amending that constitution, but something may be taken away. What assistance, what increment can be given to the provinces? No one in this House will venture for one moment to suggest that anything can be given to a single province by undertaking, ourselves, from the interior, to amend our constitution ; but on the other hand we can very easily imagine that some particular province will have some particular right taken away from it, providing the majority on the other side so desire. Where, therefore, is the gain in so far as the vital development of our nation is concerned by our having the right to amend our own constitution?

subtopic: PROPOSED CHANGE IN METHOD OF MAKING AMENDMENTS
speechtext: Would my hon. friend contend that no province is at all interested in the reform of the Senate?

subtopic: PROPOSED CHANGE IN METHOD OF MAKING AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
No, I do not contend that at all. What I do contend is this, that perhaps the reform of the Senate is a very

minor item compared with what might happen by throwing into the melting pot again the British North America Act. By deciding to submit to conferences and to the rule of the majority results might happen which would be far more serious to any province than having the Senate go forward in its present way.

subtopic: PROPOSED CHANGE IN METHOD OF MAKING AMENDMENTS
speechtext: Can we not trust ourselves?

subtopic: PROPOSED CHANGE IN METHOD OF MAKING AMENDMENTS
speechtext: Can no constitution anywhere be thrown into the melting pot? Must all constitutions remain fixed for all time?

subtopic: PROPOSED CHANGE IN METHOD OF MAKING AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
Certainly they are not fixed for all time; there is no question about that at all, but I fail to see anything that has been brought up in the course of this debate, outside perhaps of what my hon. friend for Brant (Mr. Good) has said, and which may be a source of discussion, I freely admit-I fail to see one single point that any member has brought up that would show we were suffering any injury as a whole by reason of the British North America Act. On the other hand, I do say that a province may suffer grave injustice and grave injury at the hands of the majority in the event of the British North America Act being reopened.
Then my hon. friend from Marquette spoke about the pride of national spirit. Well, I cannot understand how the right to amend the British North America Act will in any way assist in strengthening the pride in national spirit.
Another question which has been brought up in the course of this debate is whether we are or are not a nation. We are a nation for interior purposes. We might as well make up our minds immediately that we are not a nation for exterior purposes. If we are a nation for exterior purposes we have to make up our minds to undertake the responsibilities which that status involves; and if we want to call ourselves a nation, both from an interior point of view and an exterior point of view, we have not only got to provide for defence from the interior viewpoint but undertake an active part in offence from the exterior viewpoint. Are we prepared to do that? I do not think we are at the present time.
Then there were the various points my hon. friend the member for Lotbiniere (Mr. Vien) brought up in his remarks as to whether the high commissioner should 'be representative in this way or representative in that way, or whether we should be represented by an ambassador. Of what advantage would this be to us? Are we not better employed in

B.N.A. Act Amendment
minding our own business in this country, in building up this Dominion as it should be built up, and in making Canada as strong a nation interiorly as we can make it? Are we not assisting the British Empire infinitely better by, as I say, building up this country in an interior way instead of trying to dissipate our energies by interesting ourselves in various matters abroad? The time has not come, as far as I can gauge it for us to take an active and energetic interest in foreign affairs relating to the empire. Those foreign affairs at the present time, as a matter of fact, are in good hands; but for us to say that we desire to be consulted here, or we desire to be consulted there, and at the same time come forward and say " No we will not bear the responsibilities in certain ways " is simply a series of contradictions.	*
I want to repeat again what I said in the first place. As regards the events which led up to the British North America Act those events were historical, those events were drenched in blood, those events were matters of compromise of the most serious nature. I for one see nothing but difficulties ahead of us if we take it upon ourselves by conference, by act of parliament or otherwise, to attempt to change those various matters which were brought about, which took place, and which were settled by those very particular compromises. I can see no advantage to be gained but I can see disadvantages may come to certain provinces und'er certain conditions. I therefore conclude, Mr. Speaker, by saying that not only do I intend to vote against the resolution, but I also disapprove of submitting a resolution of this kind to a conference with the object in view of changing the British North America Act.

subtopic: PROPOSED CHANGE IN METHOD OF MAKING AMENDMENTS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I know that the apostles of things as they are and the disciples of subordination do not all belong to one side of the chamber. I trust that the distribution is uneven; I am sorry to see that it exists.

subtopic: PROPOSED CHANGE IN METHOD OF MAKING AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
They belong to one side
of the chamber but they sit on different sides.

subtopic: PROPOSED CHANGE IN METHOD OF MAKING AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
I have listened with a
great deal of interest to this debate in which, I may say, I had not thought I would have the privilege of taking part, but there have been some arguments advanced this afternoon to which I will endeavour to very briefly reply. I must congratulate the hon. member for St. George-St. Lawrence (Mr. Marler).

subtopic: PROPOSED CHANGE IN METHOD OF MAKING AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
You have reversed the
order.

subtopic: PROPOSED CHANGE IN METHOD OF MAKING AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
I was following the
alphabetical order, but I apologize if I made a mistake.

subtopic: PROPOSED CHANGE IN METHOD OF MAKING AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
"St. Lawrence" is the
more important saint.

subtopic: PROPOSED CHANGE IN METHOD OF MAKING AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
I think a "St. Lawrence" did not belong to the British Empire but "St. George" did. Is it loyal to prefer St. Lawrence to St. George? I have listened with some attention to what the hon. gentleman has said and I congratulate him upon his historical knowledge. But the impression made upon my mind is this, that from 1774 to 1867 we required no less than four different constitutions. Those constitutions were made for Canada, and every one except the last proved unsatisfactory. It was only when the Canadian people got together, representatives of the Maritime provinces and of the old provinces of Upper Canada and Lower Canada which then formed a United Canada -when these men got together and drafted their own constitution and had that constitution ratified by the British parliament, it was only then and not till then that we got a fairly satisfactory constitution which has remained largely unchanged for some sixty years.
May I point out a matter which I think is of some considerable interest in connection with this question. When our delegates went over to Great Britain they had, I will not say the assistance, the co-operation of British law officers in preparing different drafts of the British North America Act; and if one will read these different drafts side by side one will see some very striking dissimilarities. The British law officers said that it was in the interest of Great Britain to join the colonies of Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Canada, but that there should be a united "colony". That was the proposition in the draft of the British law officers. They used the word "colony" and they stressed the idea that the proposed union would be in the interest of the United Kingdom. The proposition in the draft of the delegates was that the provinces should not be united into one "colony". The idea of Sir John A. Macdonald was, and he belonged to the school of Tories which the hon. member for South York belongs to-

subtopic: PROPOSED CHANGE IN METHOD OF MAKING AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
Was Sir John
up-to-date?

subtopic: PROPOSED CHANGE IN METHOD OF MAKING AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
The gentleman who has led this important discussion belongs to the school of Toryism of that day. I think they called themselves Liberal-Conservatives. That is what Sir John Macdonald called himself, a Liberal-Conservative; and of the members
B.N.A. Act Amendment

of that party some are rather more liberal, others rather more conservative. The gentleman who has led this debate belongs to the more liberal wing of the Liberal-Conservative party. But the point that I want to make is that Sir John Macdonald suggested that we should be united not in one "colony" but in one "kingdom". That is the word he wished to adopt. The word "kingdom" denoted an idea not of subordination but of equality, and that is the only basis upon which I was going to say-I had almost used the expression which the rigfht hon. leader of the opposition often uses "red blooded Canadians"-it is the only status that self-respecting Canadians will enjoy.

subtopic: PROPOSED CHANGE IN METHOD OF MAKING AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
Does the hon. member
think the word "dominion" has any more *uggestion of subordination than the word 'kingdom"?

subtopic: PROPOSED CHANGE IN METHOD OF MAKING AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
I was speaking of the
fact that the choice of the word "kingdom" has a very interesting historical association. I would not say that the word "dominion" had any greater tincture of subordination than the word "kingdom"; but as we have the "United Kingdom of Great Britain" the adoption of the word "kingdom" would have seemed to put the idea of subordination perhaps more completely out of peoples minds than did the word "dominion." But it was thought by the British authorities of that time that the word "kingdom" might possibly offend the republican sensibilities of our neighbours to the south; at least that was the statement given out at the time. And they looked around for another word. Sir Leonard Tilley was reading the Psalms of David one day, and he came to the psalm where it says:
And thy dominion shall stretch from sea to sea.
"Oil" he said, "that is the word for us." And that was picked out as the word for our country, from the Psalms of David, which will have the approval of the member for George Etienne Cartier (Mr. Jacobs). I will endeavour to follow the argument of the previous speaker. His argument is against any change, and not only against any change, but against the possibility of any change, because he is afraid that difficulties may arise if a change is even suggested or discussed. He was asked I think by the hon. member for Brant (Mr. Good) "Do you regard the British North America Act as something which must always exist in its present condition?" And his answer was no. I was a little surprised at that negative, but that is what he stated. He said "The British North America Act is not like the law of the Medes and Persians. It is possible to amend it."

subtopic: PROPOSED CHANGE IN METHOD OF MAKING AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
I said that it was not
well to interfere with the British North America Act until the absolute necessity for it arose. That is what I intended to convey, and I do not think the absolute necessity exists at the present time.
Mr. MoMASTER:	That is not quite what
the hon. gentleman said when he was making his speech, but it seems to me that is a more reasonable position to 'assume. But I may reply to that in this way. If the British North America Act is susceptible of amendment under certain circumstances, which some of us may think have arisen now, and which some of us think have not arisen yet, if it is potentially amendable-I think that is the way to put it-then who should amend it? Ourselves or someone else? That is the question. There may be possible arguments of convenience about having it amended by an outside legislature who would merely ratify the agreement to which we might come. There may be some possible advantage by way of the facility with which it might be done, but I do not think that it would be wise to adopt that method, in view of the depreciation of national status which such a course would imply.

subtopic: PROPOSED CHANGE IN METHOD OF MAKING AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
Would the hon. member
define our national status?

subtopic: PROPOSED CHANGE IN METHOD OF MAKING AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
I will take that up in
a moment. I will endeavour to treat with our national status both external and internal just in a moment. If our British North America Act may have to be amended in future, then it seems to me we should be able to do it ourselves. I do not think that this parliament, the House of Commons, the Senate and the .Governor General should have the right, without references to the provinces, to change our constitution. I do not agree to that. I think it should be amended in this fashion; that after the conference in which the provinces would take their part, an agreement should be arrived at-I trust it would be arrived at-whereby we might lay down the conditions under which and the machinery by which the constitution should be amended.

subtopic: PROPOSED CHANGE IN METHOD OF MAKING AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
Who would call
that conference?

subtopic: PROPOSED CHANGE IN METHOD OF MAKING AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
I think it would be quite proper to have it called by the Prime Minister of this country. I think he would be the fit and proper person to call that conference. As a matter of fact he proposes to call a conference for one specific object, and other similar objects which phrase has been inter-

B.N.A. Act Amendment
preted by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe)-who no doubt is the legal interpreter of what the government has in its mind-to include such a subject as we have under discussion this afternoon.

subtopic: PROPOSED CHANGE IN METHOD OF MAKING AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
What protection would
the minorities have? Would they not have to trust to the fairness of the majorities?

subtopic: PROPOSED CHANGE IN METHOD OF MAKING AMENDMENTS
speechtext: Yes, if the minorities in Canada cannot trust their Canadian fellow-citizens, whom can they trust? We should not have any craven fears of any injustice being done in this country in that regard. The more we take that view I think the better for the whole people.

subtopic: PROPOSED CHANGE IN METHOD OF MAKING AMENDMENTS
speechtext: Who would decide whom the minorities must trust? The minorities themselves or whom?

subtopic: PROPOSED CHANGE IN METHOD OF MAKING AMENDMENTS
speechtext: The minorities themselves-

subtopic: PROPOSED CHANGE IN METHOD OF MAKING AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
How would a provincial
conference accomplish that? There are minorities in the different provinces.

subtopic: PROPOSED CHANGE IN METHOD OF MAKING AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
There are minorities
even in the small provinces. There may be certain minorities in Prince Edward Island.

subtopic: PROPOSED CHANGE IN METHOD OF MAKING AMENDMENTS
speechtext: There may be minorities in a province and vast majorities.

subtopic: PROPOSED CHANGE IN METHOD OF MAKING AMENDMENTS
speechtext: Does the House not realize that the people of Canada to-day are just as united as the people of sixty years ago? If reasonable provisions were made for the protection of minorities sixty years ago, is there any reasonable ground to believe that that protection will be removed by Canadians sixty years later?

subtopic: PROPOSED CHANGE IN METHOD OF MAKING AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
Who decides on the
reasonableness of the assurance? Has the minority itself not the right? Can anybody take it from them?

subtopic: PROPOSED CHANGE IN METHOD OF MAKING AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
I would presume that
in such a conference all the provinces and all elements would be represented. All the minorities in the provinces would be represented. Let me give the House an instance, from my own little county in my own province. In the last by-election we had in that county for the Quebec legislature, it was felt 'by some that it would be only fitting and right, as the county was represented by an English speaking Protestant at Ottawa that a French Roman Catholic should represent the county at Quebec. The difference in population was not more than 60 English speaking Protestants to 40 French speaking Catholics. We had the leader of the party
in power in the province of Quebec coming to the county of Brome, telling his own co-religionists and compatriots that the Protestants of Quebec had already too small a proportion of the membership in the Quebec legislature, and asking them not to change the old custom, but to see that the English speaking Protestant was elected, and he was elected. And that is the principle which has ruled us in the province of Quebec. It is the principle, I believe, whoch animates the people of Canada, and that is the spirit which we have to trust in all constitutional matters. Now the hon. member who has just resumed his seat said that in any conference the rights of a province, if any changes were made-and I do not contemplate that there would be any serious changes made-

subtopic: PROPOSED CHANGE IN METHOD OF MAKING AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
Then why take the right
to make changes?

subtopic: PROPOSED CHANGE IN METHOD OF MAKING AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
Just because I want
the right to make changes if changes are necessary, because I believe in freedom and not in restriction, because after all I am a Liberal and not a Tory, because I believe that freedom is not only good in itself, but it is the thing that has contributed more than anything else to develop our national institutions and to advance our national progress. We want to be free. Why, when the populations of many of the countries of Europe were under despotisms, it was the pride of an Englishman to say that he was a free man, a free Englishman, and he was proud of the comparative freedom of his institutions as compared with those of other countries. When Australia, the United States, Great Britain and France have the right to amend their own constitutions, I do not, for the life of me, see why Canada should not have the same right.

subtopic: PROPOSED CHANGE IN METHOD OF MAKING AMENDMENTS
speechtext: Later on in his admirable address, the hon. member will probably tell us of the obligations which freedom brings about.

subtopic: PROPOSED CHANGE IN METHOD OF MAKING AMENDMENTS
speechtext: Is the hon. member afraid of them?

subtopic: PROPOSED CHANGE IN METHOD OF MAKING AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
I will tell of the obligations which freedom brings about and' those obligations have never been declined by this country. When some ten yeans ago, it is going on now for eleven years, there came a great conflict in which we believed we were in the right and in which the peoples who were associated with us by blood on the other side of the world were also engaged, I do not believe we took refuge in any subordinate condition of our constitution to evade the
B.N.A. Act Amendment

necessities of the situation. My learned and hon. friend said this: "In a conference of the provinces of the Dominion, the provinces would inevitably lose rights and the Dominion would acquire rights."

subtopic: PROPOSED CHANGE IN METHOD OF MAKING AMENDMENTS
speechtext: Nothing of the kind.

subtopic: PROPOSED CHANGE IN METHOD OF MAKING AMENDMENTS
speechtext: I listened to my hon. friend"s remarks with great attentiveness, and my recollection of his argument is that he said it would be dangerous to have a constitutional conference because, in that constitutional conference, provinces might lose rights which they now enjoy. It is just as possible that at such conference provinces might gain rights which they do not now enjoy. If we had the right to amend the *constitution, the sovereignty being divided now between the Dominion and the provinces, if it was thought best to give to the provinces certain rights -which they do not now enjoy, it would' be quite competent to give them. If it was thought best in the interest of the whole country to take certain powers now exercised by the provinces and give them to the Dominion, that could be done as well. There is no foundation for the assertion that a conference of the provinces with the Dominion would, of necessity, result in a depreciation of the powers of the provinces.

subtopic: PROPOSED CHANGE IN METHOD OF MAKING AMENDMENTS
speechtext: Supposing that there was a conference of the dominion and the provinces and they agreed that Canada should be allowed to amend its constitution by federal act, would my hon. friend then say that this House of Commons, the Senate and the Governor General should be allowed to amend' the confederation of Canada and the provinces without reference to the provinces?

subtopic: PROPOSED CHANGE IN METHOD OF MAKING AMENDMENTS
speechtext: No, I would not. My idea would be that the provinces and ourselves should decide upon some method which required the concurrence, not only of a majority, but of a large majority of the provinces, and not only of a large majority of the provinces, but of a large majority of the people of the provinces I would have it very much along the same lines as that which gives to the American people the right to amend' their constitution. I would not have it require the concurrence of all of the provinces, because that would mean that one province could set itself up against the rest and demand better terms.

subtopic: PROPOSED CHANGE IN METHOD OF MAKING AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
On that, my hon. friend will surely not contend that if one province refuses an amendment, a majority of the others can compel it to accept such an amendment.

A contract between contracting parties cannot be amended' without the consent of all of the parties.

subtopic: PROPOSED CHANGE IN METHOD OF MAKING AMENDMENTS
speechtext: I know that and I propose to have a new contract between the Dominion and the provinces whereby, under certain conditions, changes could be made, not upon a bare majority, but upon a majority of say two-thirds, not only of the provinces themselves, but of the people of the provinces.

subtopic: PROPOSED CHANGE IN METHOD OF MAKING AMENDMENTS
speechtext: That would never be accepted.

subtopic: PROPOSED CHANGE IN METHOD OF MAKING AMENDMENTS
speechtext: If that was never accepted', the matter would fall; but I do not believe, in a progressive country, one can say: We have a constitution and we are going to make any change so difficult that it can never be changed.

subtopic: PROPOSED CHANGE IN METHOD OF MAKING AMENDMENTS
speechtext: We are a contracting party and nobody can compel us to change the contract except with the unanimous consent of the contracting parties.

subtopic: PROPOSED CHANGE IN METHOD OF MAKING AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
I agree with that
absolutely, but I would have a new contract. I was asked to speak about when Canada was a nation. According to the last speaker we are a nation for internal affairs, but not for external affairs, and it is argued that we should devote our time and attention to building up internal affairs and not bother about external affairs.

subtopic: PROPOSED CHANGE IN METHOD OF MAKING AMENDMENTS
speechtext: Or assume the responsibility.

subtopic: PROPOSED CHANGE IN METHOD OF MAKING AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
The answer I make is
that, whether we like it or not, without any control at- all upon British foreign policy, we have been exposed in the past to the hazard of war and, on the whole, whenever war has broken out, we have done our fair share. So far we have had a position of subordination that, whether we liked it or not, we have been drawn into war, and I think my hon. friend will agree with me that that is so. I doubt if there is any way which human ingenuity can devise whereby we shall have a joint control of foreign policy, but that is a question which I do not wish to enter upon at the present time. It seems to me that this question at any moment may become a practical one, although it has been regarded by some as purely theoretical. The question of the constitution of the Senate in Canada is not purely theoretical. At any time we may find the majority view of this House, as expressed by this House, as expressed by the elected representatives of the people, flouted by men

B.N.A. Act Amendment
who do not represent the people who have been appointed fotr life, the majority of whom, perhaps, have been appointed for life by a part} which represents views absolutely at variance with those held at this time by the people of Canada. Surely that is a practical question and there is ground for examining into the opportunity of changing such a situation. If we cannot examine into the wisdom of changing such a situation without an amendment to our constitution, it follows that we should have the right to amend our constitution.

subtopic: PROPOSED CHANGE IN METHOD OF MAKING AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there are one or two thoughts which I wish to express on this question as I shall have to vote against the resolution as it stands. There are some who have the idea that Britain is withholding from us something which we should have. She is not doing that; in fact, Britain is anxious, nay eager, that the overseas dominions to-day should assume and exercise the responsibilities of nationhood. There is no need yet for a change. Our dignity in the past has not suffered; in fact, I think we have in the world of commerce a prestige that we would not otherwise have had.
We should in the first place, I think, decide whether or not we want the responsibility of nationhood. The inconsistency of the whole agitation lies in this fact, that the Dominion is composed of what are or ought to be autonomous parts, and before any change can be made in the British North America Act a conference of the provinces will have to be called to decide what it is we need and desire. I shall have to vote against the resolution, because my province does not to-day stand on an equal basis with the rest of the Dominion; nor does the province of Alberta: we are treated as minors. The old provinces of Ontario and Quebec sixty years ago held these portions of the Dominion in trust until such time as their population would warrant their being formed into provinces; and that old confederation assumed the right of ownership. To-day, therefore, we are not on a footing with the rest of the provinces.

subtopic: PROPOSED CHANGE IN METHOD OF MAKING AMENDMENTS
speechtext: That is an injustice.

subtopic: PROPOSED CHANGE IN METHOD OF MAKING AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
It is an injustice which will
have to be removed before we can with any consistency ask for greater autonomy for Canada or for the full status of nationhood. The old confederation of Ontario and Quebec has dominated the rest of the Dominion since the union and has taken the means to make that domination continuous. We should have
an equal right with any other province in the Dominion to full representation in the Senate. That we have not, and until such time as our standing is secured on an equal basis with the rest of the provinces in this Dominion, I, for one, shall feel bound to vote against a resolution of this kind.
At six o'clock the House took recess.
After Recess
The House resumed at eight o'clock.

subtopic: PROPOSED CHANGE IN METHOD OF MAKING AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I had not intended to
make any observations on this subject, but so many speeches have been made with regard to it that I thought perhaps it would be proper to say a word or two.
I think everyone here must agree with the remarks of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) when he says that the British North America Act was really a treaty in which every province took part and that no important or serious changes can be made in that act except with the consent of every province interested. It seems to me that the Dominion itself is getting so set up on its greatness and power that it has lost sight of the fact, that it was the creation of the provinces, the child, so to speak, and that the provinces were the father and mother of confederation. On that fact rests an important point. Under the amendment suggested by the hon. member for South York (Mr. Maclean) it would be quite possible for this House and the Senate to amend the British North America Act in respect to any matter except, perhaps, the question of education. In other words, they could make changes in the Senate; they could change the number of representatives to be elected from the different provinces-in fact, the majority in the Senate and in the House of Commons for the time being could make any changes they wished to make. I suppose if it happened to be a Liberal majority they would take one point of view; if it was a farmer majority they might take another point of view, and if the Conservative party was in power they might take a totally different attitude. So it seems to me that the proposal as presented to the House is not fair or practicable so far as the provinces which formed the confederation are concerned. I cannot see anything in the suggestion beyond this: It seems perfectly evident that if the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) calls a conference of the Dominion and the provinces, he will not be able to get anywhere unless the
B.N.A. Act Amendment

consent of all the provinces is obtained. That is, of course, assuming that they are willing to accept the argument of the Minister of Justice that all the provinces must consent to any change that is to be made-a practice, I believe, which has prevailed ever since confederation. So that even if the provinces did get together and we had the power in this parliament to make the desired amendments, the only difference is that we would not have to send them over to England and say to the imperial authorities: "The Dominion and the provinces are desirous of having a change made in the act; this is what they want; will you kindly put it through?" That is about what it amounts to; because I have not heard anyone suggest that the British government has ever objected to any of the slight amendments that have been made to the act at our request. It seems to me, therefore, that there is practically nothing in the proposal.
Some reference has been made to the de-sirablity of having a Canadian ambassador at Washington. Well, I think that at this time we need the backing of the 'whole British Empire at Washington. For some time the city of Chicago has been taking large quantities of the waters of the Great Lakes. This is not a legal question at all; it is something like the case of two farmers living side by side-one of them cannot take more than his proper share of the water of a river running between the two farms. For years they have been taking this water, which belongs as much to Canada as it does to the United States, and they have been running it down into the Mississippi and utilizing it in the production of power. It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that it is high time for this country to take the position as part of the British Empire that not one foot of water should go through Chicago from the Great Lakes down into the Mississippi. It is not, as I have said a legal matter; it is not a question of a treaty. But that water is our property, and the government of this country should get busy in the matter. Do not bother with an ambassador at Washington, but say to the British govem-men: "Look here; get into this. We will help you by supporting the British navy instead of sponging upon you as we have done for a hundred and fifty years." If you get the British Empire as a whole behind you perhaps you will get something done. They might tell the United States: "We will not pay you anything more until you get that difficulty with this part of the British Empire settled." Great Britain is paying millions to the United States every year; it is the only country in the world that is paying its war

debts, and we should get the whole British Empire together shaking its fists in a pleasant and agreeable way at Washington, and saying: We want that water back. It is costing us millions of dollars to deepen our canal system and our ports because of the water they are taking down there, and we sit calmly here and waste our time in this debate which might better have been conducted in a school with a prize for the one who makes the best speech. It gets us nowhere. The thing we want to remember is that we are a part of the British Empire, and we Want to stick to the British Empire. We do not want to bother with a Canadian ambassador at Washington; we want the whole British Empire behind this country all the time. I cannot see what particular happiness or pleasure any man in this country gets over the signing of a treaty with the United States by our own plenipotentiary, when we allow the British people to pay practically the whole cost of the British navy. We are not commencing to pay our share of the cost of the defence of this country; at no cost to us we have been defended by the British navy for a hundred and fifty years.
What made the United States break away from England? It was simply because England started to put a small tax on the United States, which had been in existence as a British colony for a hundred years. A small tax was put on practically for the purpose of defending their coasts so that they could become a great and prosperous country, and the colony thereupon broke away from the Mother Country, and as soon as it became prosperous it started in to have a rebellion of its own. Are we going to allow the British people to pay the whole cost of the British navy until we become prosperous, and then say: We do not need the British navy; we are going to run our own country. Fortunately, we have not arrived at that stage yet. I think it is time we recognized our position as part of the British Empire. Great Britain having learned a lesson from the breaking away of the United States will not attempt to put a tax on us, but are we going to allow the British people to pay the whole cost of that navy which defends our coasts and allows us to become great and prosperous? It is time that we paid our share, instead of running a little artificial navy. Who wants to get on ships in this country? No one that I know of. People can make so much more money on land that they would rather stay on shore and make money. The British navy is for the defence of the whole empire, and as we do not want to go on ships and have a navy of our own.

B.N.A. Act Amendment
as we want to stay ashore, like the Americans, and make money, it is only fair that we should pay our share. That is what we should be considering, instead of whether we should have the power to change the British North America Act. When we want any change made we have simply to ask Great Britain to make the change, and Ae will do it.

subtopic: PROPOSED CHANGE IN METHOD OF MAKING AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, those who have in this debate, up to now, sided with the mover of this amendment, have to their credit the fact of having strived for the principle of self-government, but is this principle of autonomy referred to by the supporters of the hon. member for South York (Mr. Maclean), the only one which must be taken into consideration by this House? I think there is another principle which certainly demands our consideration, and it is, that the privileges which were granted to us by the British North America Act are part of a sacred pact not to be altered or amended by a majority in the House of Commons. The Fathers of Confederation, at the time, in order to obtain the full co-operation of our compatriots of the various provinces, offered the following guarantee, that under the control of both the Commons and Senate, certain vested rights would be maintained in favour of the various nationalities lit the provinces. The British North America Act was enacted by the Fathers of Confederation, after a number of meetings and much discussion, and this Act created the general impression, in this country, that it was the safeguard of our traditions and vested rights, especially for the old provinces of Lower and Upper Canada. It is because they believed that this principle was embodied in the British North America Act, that the various provinces welcomed Confederation and, since 1867, joined it of their own free will. The present generations, like the one of 1867, wish to maintain for these nationalities in the various provinces of Confederation, the same pledges in regard to their vested rights and sound traditions.
The resolution which is submitted to us, while evidencing a desire not to wound the feelings of the provinces interested in this confederation pact, nevertheless introduces an element of a nature to diminish the safeguards which we possess, is a source of anxiety and apprehension to the various component groups.	So far as I am concerned, the great confidence which I place in confederation, under the high protection of the British crown, the faith I repose in it as an upholder of the traditions and the vested rights of the French population co-operating
with the English in this country for the good administration of the Dominion, this reliance I could not place in the legal status which the present motion tends to establish, because with such a legal status the various nationalities in the provinces would be at the mercy of the changeable and often ill-inspired views of the majorities holding power in parliament. This is why I am opposed to the motion to amend our constitution.
The Confederation Act of 1867, in the eyes of the provinces, is a sacred one which must always remain intact. It gives us rights to which we are attached, it strongly contributes to the maintenance of peace and harmony in this country, it is the shield of our customs and rights, and, it is because it remains unaltered that the provinces adhere to the pact It would therefore be, in my opinion, a mistake for this House to assume the right to change or amend it at will.
Moreover, we have, in this country, existed! as a confederation for almost sixty years. Since the year 1867, the provinces have been united, forming a confederation pact under the aegis of this British North America Act. Since then have we had occasion to complain? On any occasion when the Canadian people expressed a wish to amend their constitution, have they ever been denied that right, by the British Crown? Have we any reason to believe that in future the British crown might be guilty of injustice towards us. Whatever may be the very sincere considerations which have prompted the movers of this resolution, I cannot help considering as a slur on the Imperial authorities, the fact that some among us wish, after sixty years of existence, to claim the power to amend our constitution. It looks as if we wished to tell them that we had no further confidence in their authority, that we have special reasons to complain; as if, in the course of these sixty years, we had been requesting of the British crown amendments to our constitution which they had refused! Now, Sir, Canada is not in that position; it is fully satisfied with the charter obtained in 1867, which has contributed to the development of our country, safeguarded autonomy in all the provinces and largely helped to maintain this harmony so necessary to the welfare of the country; the Canadian people are happy to possess such a charter, because it is a pledge of peace and harmony; a safeguard of the traditions and vested rights which are theirs.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: PROPOSED CHANGE IN METHOD OF MAKING AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
Before a vote is taken on
B.N.A. Act Amendment

the amendment to the amendment which has been moved by my hon. friend the member for East Calgary (Mr. Irvine) I should like to point out that there seems to be three entirely distinct and separate questions which have come to the fore in this discussion and which, if I may be permitted to say so, are being more or less confused. The resolution of my hon. friend (Mr. Maclean, York) as drafted, gives rise to them in a natural way. It is important we should see that the consideration of any one of thie three questions does not necessarily involve a like point of view with respect to the others.
There is in the first place the question of the right to amend our own constitution, a question which one might describe at present as theoretical or academic, although it may come to have in the course of time some very practical bearings. There is secondly the question of the method by which this country should proceed to secure amendment of its constitution should it decide such a step to be desirable and necessary. There are two methods that have been suggested. One is contained in the resolution of my hon. friend to the effect that a resolution of both houses of parliament should be addressed to His Majesty the King praying the British parliament to amend the constitution in the manner set forth. As has been pointed out in setting forth the other method, that method ignores altogether the relationship of the provinces to the Dominion in the creation of the constitution itself. All of that particular phase of the question was so fully and conclusively argued by the Minister of Justice yesterday that this House, I believe, is practically unanimously of the view that if an amendment of the kind is to 'be sought, due regard should be had to the view that a compact was made at the time of confederation, and that an amendment of the importance that such an amendment certainly would have, ought only to be proposed after there had been a conference and agreement between the Dominion and the provinces.
The third question which has come up in discussion, and which seems to be entirely separate and distinct from each of the others, is, assuming the House or the country has come to the decision that the constitution should be amended in a manner which would permit of its amendment within the boundaries of our country, so to speak, without going beyond to apply to the British parliament, and assuming that we had agreed upon the method by which the British parliament should be approached in that regard, what then are to be the terms of the amendment 
itself? What are to be the conditions by which the people of Canada, when they come to amend their constitution, shall be prepared to abide in any amendment they may have under consideration. Perhaps I can illustrate this point by a reference to the resolution of my hon. friend. The third clause in the resolution says.
" The proposed law for the alteration of the said act must be passed by an absolute majority of each house of parliament."
My hon. friend says that if the constitution is to be amended at any time it must be by a majority of this House and of the Senate. Some hon. members who have participated in the discussion have thought that instead of a bare majority, a two-thirds majority might be required. If not a two-thirds majority in all cases possibly a two-thirds majority in some cases, and a simple majority in others. All I wish to point out at the moment is that the question of terms or conditions is a question apart altogether from what I believe to be the question the hon. member for South York wished to have discussed, namely-whether the constitution of Canada might upon terms and conditions to be agreed upon, be amended within the confines of Canada itself, and without the necessity of any request to the British parliament to make the amendment. I would feel that my hon. friend's motion as it stands could not be accepted for the reason, if for no other, that it is, inadvisable for this House at this time to commit itself as to the terms or conditions on which any amendment should be made to the constitutions; very full opportunity at the right moment should be afforded for considering and discussing that important feature. Similarly I would feel that my hon. friend's motion should not pass this House, even in the amended form namely, providing that the consent of the provinces must be obtained, without in the first instance permitting the provinces to confer with the Dominion with respect to the address that should be presented to His Majesty.
May I add one word in regard to the amendment to the amendment which has been moved by my hon. friend for East Calgary because I think it, too, helps to illustrate the confusion, which has arisen in the discussion of this matter. My hon. friend suggests that the resolution should be amended by adding to sub-section 2 the words:
And that before further action be taken on the proposed resolution the same be referred to the consideration of the conference proposed in the Speech from the Throne for consideration and recommendation.

B.N.A. Act Amendment
I do not know whether my hon. friend for East Calgary has noticed' that what he is proposing to do is to ask the two Houses of parliament to send a petition to His Majesty praying that the British House will amend the constitution in the way the member for South York has suggested with the words of ' my hon. friend for East Calgary included. The resolution of my hon friend from South York is: That a humble address be presented to His Most Excellent Majesty in the following words-and the words which my hon. friend from East Calgary has moved as an amendment are part of the words which under his amendment are to go into the address to be presented to His Majesty the King. I am sure my hon. friend the member for East Calgary never intended and does not wish anything of the kind; that, nevertheless, is the effect of his amendment. For that reason, Mr. Speaker, I do not think my hon. friend's amendment will appeal to the House. I am equally sure it will not appeal to himself once he sees its effect.
The point at issue, it seems to me, narrows a'own to whether or not this country should have the right to amend its own constitution, without in that connection asking any assistance of the British parliament. In a discussion of this kind I think we ought to have regard for the impression which our words within these walls may create in the minds of those who may read them beyond the precincts of this parliament. The simple discussion of whether or not we should have the right to amend our constitution may be differently interpreted. Some persons reading this debate, or possibly reading the headlines of the debate as they will doubtless appear in the press in different parts of the world, would assume that this parliament, or rather that the people of Canada had not the right to amend their own constitution. Very much depends upon what we mean when we use the word " right " in that connection. I contend, Mr. Speaker, that we have the right to amend our constitution; and I will not go further than the resolution of my hon. friend for South York (Mr. Maclean) to give the House evidence that at least, we think we have that right. By his resolution my hon. friend is proposing that we should amend' the constitution, and he is taking what he believes to be the constitutional method of securing an amendment. We could not amend' our own constitution in the manner in which my hon. friend suggests, if we had not that right; and yet this discussion might create the impression abroad' that the people of Canada have not the right to amend their constitution. I do not profess to have very
much knowledge of constitutional law, but I recall at the moment a distinction made by constitutional authorities which I think is pertinent to the present discussion; and that is the distinction made between what is referred to as the law of the constitution and the conventions of the constitution. So eminent an authority as Dicey on the law of the constitution, as I remember his writing, has intimated that even a lawyer pursuing the study of the law of the constitution into a consideration of the conventions of the constitution would come to see that he had but proceeded a little further on the one path.
So far as the letter of the law is concerned, the Canadian people, technically speaking, have not the right or power to amend the constitution without asking the British parliament to pass a law for that purpose and without the consent of the British parliament. If that were taken to imply that the British parliament itself might, whenever it wished to do so, amend our constitution without any reference to Canada, or that the British parliament, when it was requested so to do might with respect to an amendment refuse to carry out the wishes of the Canadian people, then we might say that we had not the right to amend our own constitution; that some other body, namely, the British parliament possessed that right. But where the facts are as we know them to be that this parliament approaching the British parliament in a constitutional and regular way, by an address of both Houses requesting any amendment to our constitution, will have the amendment carried out in accordance with its wishes, it cannot be said that we have not the right or the power to amend our constitution. We have both. I contend, Mr. Speaker, that the conventions of the constitution are just as important and binding as the law in a matter of this kind, and that the convention governing the amendment of the Canadian constitution to-day is that whenever the people of Canada proceed in a constitutional way to ask the British parliament as their	agent-because it is
practically as their agent that they ask the British parliament to do this-to amend the constitution in a particular way, the British parliament will always proceed so to act in accordance with that request. That being the case, this country has the full constitutional right to amend its constitution.
The real question at issue narrows down therefore, to a very small compass, namely to whether we desire in Canada to amend our own constitution, confining the transaction strictly within the boundaries of the Dominion, or whether we would rather main-
B.N.A. Act Amendment

tain the procedure which is essential at the present time in consequence of the historical facts and circumstances governing the matter, namely, of proceeding beyond the boundaries of the Dominion to the Mother Country to ask the British parliament to make the desired amendment in accordance with the expressed wish of our own constituted authorities. Now that is a question that seems to admit of discussion. There is much to be said on both sides. Personally I cannot but feel that for a number of reasons it would be preferable to save the British parliament, in connection with its business, growing as it is from day to day, the necessity, of troubling itself with respect to any matters which are distinctively a part of our own self government. I appreciate the feeling, I think it is a natural feeling, that many citizens of this country have, that the Dominion holding the position it does in all other particulars should not suffer under even a theoretical limitation in this particular matter. So far as I am concerned, I confess I do not see in it at the moment anything more than a theoretical limitation. There is no practical problem that has arisen up to the present time that I am aware of that in this regard has occasioned the necessity for any sudden action on the part of the Parliament of Canada. I think it is all important that this should be made perfectly clear, that it should be understood in the Old Country as well as here, that so far as the Old Country is concerned, we know that Britain is prepared to do in this matter whatever the people of Canada may wish to have done, and that if no change has come about thus far, or if the situation is what it is at the moment, it is, as has been said many times in the course of this debate, entirely of our own creation I think the further fact should be made clear, namely, that as a people we cannot be held to be making any sort of a complaint or entertaining a grievance with respect to the existing situation, but rather that this discussion is one practically, as has been said to-day, largely academic in character. That being the case, Mr. Speaker, it seems to me the question is one which very properly would come before a conference to be arranged by the government between the federal and provincial authorities, such a conference as in the Speech from the Throne it has been announced it is the intention of the government to call. I hope that with the assurance to my hon. friend, seeing that the matter has elicited the attention it has in this House in the last day or two, that the government will make it one of the subjects to be referred to such a conference, he will see the wisdom of not pressing his resolution to a vote, 
but will feel that he has already served the very admirable purpose which I am sure he had in view in making the motion, namely that of creating that interest in discussion and otherwise which is most essential to an adequate consideration of this important question.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. ARTHUR MEIGHEN (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: PROPOSED CHANGE IN METHOD OF MAKING AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
The presence of the hon. member for South York (Mr. Maclean) accompanying this motion assures it a respectful hearing on the part of members of this House. The hon. gentleman has enjoyed for some years the distinction of being the oldest parliamentarian in this Dominion, and enjoys as well a position of high esteem among all members of the House of Commons.
I am afraid I cannot congratulate him on the degree of unanimity with which his resolution now before us has been received in favour by members of parliament. Whatever [DOT]importance the motion may have, the discussion of it has had this shattering result; it has split the Labour party in two. Their views are now so multiplied that the rest of us cannot present an amendment at all. I have no hesitation in coming to a conclusion as to the merits of the motion and both amendments. I would not make any request of the hon. member for South York. So far as I am concerned the pressing of the resolution to a division is a matter entirely within his own pleasure. With some regret, so far as he is personally concerned, I have to say at the outset, that I will vote decisively against the motion, the amendment and the sub-amendment.
A part of the discussion, I think, has not been very relevant, and I say that with all deference to previous speakers. I do not think we have before us anything that touches, even remotely, the question of the wisdom of preserving an appeal to the Privy Council. My view on that question I may indicate later, but the subject has no relation to the motion before the House. The hon. member who moves this resolution referred to it some days ago and lodged a complaint that the law lords of the Privy Council had shot holes through the constitution of Canada. If they have, their action is wholly null because they were never vested with such power. It is their duty, if appeal is made, to decide what the meaning of the British North America Act is. That, in the case in dispute, the appeal on the Industrial Disputes Act, they did and they gave their reasons therefor. I think it is unfortunate that there should be anything in the nature

B.N.A. Act Amendment
of an attack because of that judgment. For myself, I would have deprecated the carrying of the case to the Privy Council, indeed, into litigation at all. I believe it has been the balance of opinion of the Justice department for many years that if the Lemieux Act, so-called, got into the courts, its fate was very doubtful, indeed, was probably sealed. I have no reason to think they have varied that view in the present instance, and I think the carrying of the Industrial Disputes Act case in the matter of the Hydro-Electric Commission employees was an impetuous adventure from which we have returned in discomfiture with nothing left but a feeling of remorse and a bill of expense.
But all this has nothing to do with the case before us. We have to vote "yes" or "no" to a resolution, an amendment and a sub-amendment, and in determining what we do, we must read each of the three, because our vote, if in the affirmative, means support of whatever one we vote for as it reads. It does not mean support of some more or less nebulous principle which we think the mover may have in the back of his head.
The resolution itself calls upon this House to petition they British parliament to give us power to amend the British North America Act by a majority vote. I have not heard any hon. member, save the mover, support the resolution in those naked terms. The speech of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) is decisive in the negative. He raised only the one objection-no other is needed. He laboured it, perhaps, too long, but he presented it most forcibly and well. No one in this parliament of Canada could dream, for a moment, of asking the British House of Commons and House of Lords to tear up the securities to which we and others are parties on the mere demand of this House itself. Undoubtedly, the pact of confederation is a contract and there are rights involved therein not represented by the Parliament of Canada. We could not put ourselves in the position of asking that rights so secured should be disturbed on our motion alone. The speech of the Minister of Justice determines, I think, without power of dispute, that there should never be suggestion of amendment affecting other parties to the contract save after conference and consent of those other parties. As he delivered that speech, I could not help regretting that he had not made it before the famous challenge of the powers of the Senate which rang through this chamber last July. I could not help regretting that he had not made it in the hearing of the Prime Minister before he went through western Canada and delivered those blood-and-thunder speeches about curtailing the authority of the upper house. There was no suggestion then while he was on the stu'inps of western Canada about a conference of the provinces before this assault on the Senate was to be made.

speechtext:
One is not able to tell
what is contemplated by the actual words of the Prime Minister when on the stump. That threat, however, is now reduced to the suggestion of a conference which, I think we are all pretty ready to admit, means nothing more than a kiss good-bye to the whole terrible campaign. So much for the resolution.
The amendment of the hon. member for Winnipeg (Mr. Woodsworth) is more cautious, It is to the effect that we shall petition for power to amend at our will within certain limits the British North America Act, but shall do so only after having obtained the consent of all of the provinces of Canada. Even then the amendment proposes that we have authority to change only within the limits of a rather contracted circle. We are not to ask even with the approval of all the provinces for unlimited power of amendment, we are to ask only for power to amend in so far as we can do so without interference with minority rights. This is the undoubted result of the language in which the amendment appears as suggested by the hon. member for Centre Winnipeg. In the first place, I do not think it would be a matter of convenience that the whole of the provinces of Canada should in every case consent. If we are going to put those obstacles in front of our course, we are going to add to the difficulties if any did exist, that we have had in the past. We have amended the British North America Act many times upon address of this House without speaking to the provinces at all. Why? Because the amendments we asked for did not affect in any way minority rights, did not affect in the remotest way provincial rights, were amendments in which the provinces or minorities were not concerned at all. It would be cumbersome indeed in such cases to be compelled to pass first from province to province and obtain universal approval. Besides, I do not think we are going to gain anything in the world by asking for power to be vested in this House to amend, in relation to one sphere, a constitutional right while, in relation to another sphere, we must
B.N.A. Act Amendment

pursue the course we have pursued in years gone by. It seems to me that then would develop an anomalous situation and it is merely fanciful and illusory for us to dream that, after we have such result, our status would be in the least elevated or that we would be more of a nation than we aTe today.
The third amendment moved by the hon. member for East Calgary (Mr. Irvine) has, I think, in effect, the interpretation given to it by the Prime Minister. If the hon. member for East Calgary agrees, I am satisfied that he will not himself ask that we shall vote upon this amendment. I know he did not intend such effect. If I have his puipose aright, he intended that we should express ourselves the opinion that this parliament should have the right to amend the British North America Act, but that we should not convey that opinion to the British House until the provinces of Canada agree. To that also I am emphatically opposed. I do not think this parliament should have the right of its own will and motion, under any conditions, without reference to the provinces, even though they might presently grant us that right, to amend in any way we choose the British North America Act. Though the provinces might agree that we should go to the British House and ask for the right to be vested in this parliament alone, I would not be a party to the assertion of such a right. There are, in this Dominion, minorities whom no provincial legislature distinctly represents. The voice of those minorities is heard even in the midst of this debate. Are we to assume that because certain legislatures, which do not speak for those minorities, tell us to take to ourselves the right to amend the British North America Act at will we ought, therefore, to do so? I do not think so at all. So that, in the form which the three propositions now before the House take, I could not vote for any of them.
There still remains, however, the question at large, should we seek by some channel or other to obtain these powers? It perhaps is not worth discussing in so far as deciding the vote of any one on what is before us is concerned, but it has been discussed and I do not want to evade it in any degree whatever.
I am afraid myself that if we launch very far into this question and seek to set up some other method than that already pursued we are only going to get further and further into the morass; and any substitute which we are able to invent will be far more cumbersome and even less dignified than that to which we have subscribed through all these

years. We differ from Australia and South Africa. We are a federation of a variety of minorities and majorities. A suggestion has been made, I believe, by Sir Clifford Sifton,- and I cannot help but note the more brotherly language and Christian spirit in which his name is spoken of by hon. gentlemen opposite now than characterized similar references just a few years ago,-that there should be some divisions created throughout the Dominion and some proportional representation election; and that the delegates so elected should re-draft our constitution. Well, it seems to me that if such were done the very securities that now prevail would be insisted on again. There is no reason in the world to assume that any different securities could be substituted. And why is this the case? Simply because you cannot erect any structure of balances and referendums as simple and effective as the method which obtains to-day. Imagine an agreement to which any minority in this country could logically be asked to subscribe, an agreement under which there would be a reference to the provinces and then a reference to minorities, all entailing weeks and months, perhaps years of labour, all giving rise to disputations and controversies, section against section-that is to say, if the change proposed amounted to anything at all. Imagine a system such as that to which any of the various minorities of Canada would likely subscribe at any conference! No matter how you go about it, whether by a new system of divisions or by the legislatures as they exist in conjunction with this parliament, you will arrive ultimately at just the same difficulty which confronted the Fathers of Confederation and which they surmounted by the instrumentality of the British North America Act.
Is it all worth while? Are we going to be any better off after this is all done than we are now? The answer comes in the speeches we have heard this very day. One hon. gentleman, even the mover himself, rises and says: "All I ask for, and I ask it in the name of the dignity and nationhood of Canada, is that in matters which do not affect minorities we shall have the right to amend our constitution". And he declares that to the outside world our status will be enhanced; it will all appear a whole lot better to 9 p.m. the world at large, who will look on us as higher in rank among the nations, more independent, more autonomous, less subordinate to the Motherland. I do not follow this reasoning at all. If we would still have in all important cases to go through the circuitous journey which we take now,

B.N.A. Act Amendment
why should we not do the same in every instance? If the outside world sees us take this course in all matters of consequence, I do not think that we are likely to be elevated to any position of superior dignity because we do not have to submit to the same necessity in matters which are merely minor. The hon. member for Lotbiniere (Mr. Vien) says that there are certain subjects which he never would commit for decision to the Parliament of Canada, no matter who else might consent to this being done. We rest, says he, on the security which is found in the British parliament so far as these particular matters are concerned. But, says the hon. member, as to other subjects, "for the sake of our position before the world, I beg of you to adopt some new means whereby we can change the act at will". For the life of me I do not see anything to be gained at all so long as there is something reserved.
But if there were nothing reserved, if all minorities would agree to something definite -and this to my mind is purely visionary- if all were unanimous that we abandon recourse to the British parliament altogether, and, through some system at home, vest in the various legislatures and the Parliament of Canada the right to amend the constitution, would we really be further ahead than we are now? The Prime Minister says, and I support him to the full, that we have today an absolute constitutional right to fix the terms of our constitution. Speaking for the people of Canada, satisfying the British parliament that we so speak-and there is no difficulty in doing this if the voice of objection is not heard-we have the right as a parliament to decide what goes into that act and what stays out. Such is our position to-day. Hon. gentlemen say: "Yes, but that only rests on the foundation of constitutional right; by law we still have to go around the route to the British parliament, and we do not want to rest on the insecure basis of mere constitutional right. We want our legal rights plainly defined' before the world." Let us inquire into that contention. In my judgment our legal position would not be one whit the stronger in that case than it is now. True, it is by virtue of constitutional right that we can now dictate virtually any amendments to the act, provided we speak for all Canada and the voice of minorities raises no objection. But the sanction of constitutional right within this British Empire is just as firm, just as lasting and just as dependable as the voice of law itself. But I go farther. When we have gone through all this and got our substituted system, when we have obtained the 22
legal right to amend in our several parliaments this British North America Act, the legal foundation is not one iota better than it was before. Why do I say that? Though the British North America Act may be amended, in such a way as to give the Parliament of Canada, after a long series of provincial approvals, the right to amend the act, after that is all done the legal power would still remain in the British parliament to change the act at will. And nothing could restrain them save a regard for constitutional authority. In other words, we would still be protected by constitutional right and constitutional right alone; the legal power in the British parliament would remain to amend the act or to repeal it. So that after all the sanction we would have would be the very sanction we now enjoy. The legal right exists to-day, for example, on the part of His Majesty to veto any act of the Parliament of Great Britain. Though the legal right exists, however, the constitutional right has died; it is antiquated and obsolete and virtually does not exist at all. And it would be just as true to say that the Parliament of Great Britain to-day is a mere instrument and tool of monarchy as it is to say that this parliament, speaking for the people of Canada, has not the right to amend our constitution. We have the right, and before the world we could be no better off or better protected if any scheme whatever of the nature now proposed were adopted.
I may be old fashioned in this matter and if I am I will take the consequences. But I am not very anxious to strip the British Empire of those emblems of unity which today dignify it before the face of the world. I do not want to do anything of the kind unless there is something to be gained, something material and practical beyond all that is lost. For my own part I think we have travelled far enough along this road. Rather, I believe that it has-on ourselves and on the world without-a wholesome effect to see these visible signs of our unity remain, to see our appeal to the Privy Council preserved, to see our power of amendment exercised through the old British parliament; to see in a word that the British Empire is the British Empire still.

Mr. Speaker, I do not want to get the House into a muddle over this question; I want to see that due respect is paid both to the House and to the question itself.

Lawyers can put up arguments on all kinds of cases, and we have a good many lawyers in this House. The Minister of Justice led the lawyers who spoke on this question, and the leader of the opposition followed the same line as the Prime Minister-they are all trying to get past the issue. They forget that we are living alongside the United States, a great country which has achieved something in the way of better conditions for the world. Some people may say they have not entirely succeeded; perhaps not. But they have done something. Out of a condition similar to ours they evolved a constitution which they themselves have power to amend. They have amended it, and have continued to amend it. Instead of being governed as they were in the first place by the thirteen original states, they are now governed by the senate and congress of the United States. In other words, the people of the United States can make, amend and interpret their own constitution. But leading members of this House, especially its legal lights, say that in that respect Canada is helpless; we cannot do it. As a Canadian I resent that doctrine, and I hope I shall live long enough to see a change made.
I did hope to hear something from my friends down to the left, the Progressives. They know they have grievances; I have heard them mention them within the last two or three days. We have a right to make our own court and to express our confidence in it. Now am I a disloyal Canadian in saying that? A lot of these electors in York township that I spoke of are market gardeners and fruit growers, and these market gardeners and fruit growers in the township of York believe in 22i

I am British enough to think that what is good enough for the great Mother Country is good enough for Canada, especially when it is good enough for Australia and even for the new state of South Ireland. The State of South Ireland is not limited in a single direction in the amending of its constitution, except in one respect; it cannot wipe out the king's prerogative; the king is the head of the state. This new state has absolute autonomy in every direction excepting that one thing. Australia also has the same right, and they are vindicating it. Are they disloyal for that? Yet he has been trying to say that in the most pedantic way; I never heard such a pedantic speech as he made this afternoon. He endeavoured to say I was disloyal in such an insinuating way. He is a clever lawyer; I give him credit for that. But it is absurd to say that we in this country of ours, and that your sons and my sons after we are gone, are not to have a say as Canadians in the framing of the constitution of Canada, and I say that with all respect to my fellow countrymen of Quebec and other portions of Canada which have guaranteed rights in our constitution.
I presented only a skeleton proposition to the House.
