When a proposition of this kind comes up we have to sit in this House and listen to the best lawyers we have, in the person of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) and in the leader of the opposition, a gentleman for whom I have the greatest respect-I think he is the ablest parliamentarian in this country-but he is not in accord, he does not mesh to-day with the hon. member for South York on this question. Having this proposition before us, I have no doubt that the Parliament of Canada, made up

Mr. E. R. E. CHEVRIER moved the second reading of Bill No. 2, to amend and 'make operative certain provisions of the 'Copyright Act, 1921.

I do not pretend to
know very much about the law nor about the Copyright Act as it stands, but I do know
Copyright Act Amendment

this, that very strong representation has been made against this measure, and it seems to me that before the second reading is passed, which virtually confirms the principle of the bill, the state of the law should be briefly expounded, the effect of the amendment briefly explained and the judgment of hon. members who have followed this law given for the benefit of us all.

In view of the statement that has just been made as to the opinions of lawyers, I feel rather diffident about expressing an opinion now, but I quite agree with the words of the right hon. the leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen) that the copyright law is at present a very complicated matter. If I had to quote authority for that I would refer to the debates that took place in this House and in the Senate in 1921 and 1923 when a number of distinguished members took part in the discussion including some ministers and ex-ministers, and the statement was made that nobody in this House apparently understood this law. It is rather a difficult situation to be placed in to be asked now to explain this law, but I think a synopsis can be given in a very few words. In 1886, at Berne, a convention was arrived at relating to international copyrights in which the leading nations of the world took part and became adherents to that convention. Britain was one of the parties to the Berne convention and extended to Canada the operation of this international copyright law. Canada nevertheless had its own domestic copyright law, chapter 88 of 30 Victoria, 1875. In 1908 the Convention of Berne was revised. Britain continued to adhere thereto, but did not extend the dispositions thereof to Canada. It was not until 1921 that the present Copyright Act was passed, containing most of the dispositions of the Berne convention but containing contrary to the convention the licensing clauses. The object of this bill is to correct these objectionable features, which are objectionable to those for whose benefit the copyright law was first instituted. I refer to sections 12, 13 and 15. Moreover, all through the act definitions have been left out as well as means of remedy. There have been omitted also certain rights of authors, of printers and of people who may enjoy the benefit of the reproduction of works. After all the main point at issue is really the repeal of the licensing clauses. It would be presumption on my part to endeavour to explain the intricacies of this legislation at this time, although if the House will bear with me I will endeavour to do so.

If the House will permit, I think the best way of dealing with this legislation will be to submit it to a special committee. When this law came up in 1923 it was discussed fully, and I find the hon. member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie) stated at that time:
In the meantime my suggestion to the minister in this matter would be, seeing the bill is going to raise a good deal of controversy upon very difficult points, to refer the measure to a small select committee, (representative of the different parties in the House, and ask the authors, the publishers and the printers to state their case.
Then the hon. member for South Simcoe (Mr. Boys) said:
I would like to support the suggestion of the hon. *member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie) that a small select committee be at once appointed.
And then later on in the debate the suggestion was repeated.	This time the hon.
member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie) said:
I was satisfied when the bill was up before, and I am just as firmly satisfied now that apart from the minister himself there is not a man in the committee at this present moment who understands this legislation.
Further on, he said:
I have tried to g6t to ' the bottom of this matter;
I have spent a lot of time on it and I confess I do not fully understand it now. My suggestion to the minister, when the bill was last up, was that he appoint a small committee, as was done in 1921, before whom the authors, publishers and printers can appear and state their claims. The committee will have to go to the bottom of the matter and report on this bill. I understood that my suggestion on that occasion agreed with the view of the minister. The hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Forke) backed up the proposal very emphatically. He said that he did not understand it, that the committee did not either, and he refused to commit himself to legislation which he did not understand. I do not know anything quite as complicated or quite as involved as the copyright question.
He requested that a committee be appointed. For the same reasons I now ask that the consideration of this bill be left to a special committee.

Mr. Speaker, my attention was not called to this bill until a moment ago, and I have just had an opportunity of glancing over it very hurriedly. I remember when the bill was before the House some two years ago. At that time I took some interest in it and some part in the discussion, and I think my hon friend (Mr. Chevrier) has correctly quoted me. The opinion which I then held, I still hold, that this, bill deals with one of the most involved and intricate matters that can come up for consid'eration by this parliament. I am quite satisfied that the proper mode of procedure is by a special committee. Personally, I would have no objection whatever

Copyright Act Amendment
to the motion that this bill be referred to a special committee. I see that the very sections which, after a great deal of consideration and much discussion, we enacted two years ago, the present measure seeks now to repeal. I know that as soon as the fact becomes generally known throughout Canada that it is the intention to repeal those sections, many interests which are now d'ormant will take an interest in the matter, and one of them in particular. The effect of the amendment, as I am able to determine it from a mere glance at the provisions, is to change those provisions of our former act which compelled the manufacture of the literary work in the Dominion of Canada. The object of the main section of the former bill was to compel the manufacture or the printing of the literary work in this country under a system of license which was approved by the House at that time. The main object of the present bill is to take away that protection which we then afforded to the printing establishments and printers of this country and to allow authors to have their works printed' in foreign countries and sent into Canada on particularly favourable terms. I do not wish to be one of those who are going to assent to the principle of this bill at present; but subject to that, I think the hon. member who has introduced the bill has taken the proper course in asking that it be referred to a special committee of this House.

Mr. Speaker, before this bill goes to a committee, I should like the House to understand its significance. As my hon. friend has stated, this bill was passed in 1921, but it was found' that in one particular it infringed the provisions of the Berne convention, so the act was not brought into operation. But in 1923, as you will see if you examine a copy of the bill, certain amendments were made to bring it within the Berne convention. My hon. friend has told the House that the bill bears hardly upon the authors. I do not think he can maintain that position. At the present time a Canadian author who sells his work to a United States publisher must throw in his Canadian rights. Und'er this law he may throw in his Canadian rights, but unless the American publisher publishes the book in Canada, some other publisher may take it and print it; but if he does so, the author must be paid for that. Therefore, if his work is sold to the United States and published on this sid'e by another publisher, the author gets not only his price from the American publisher, but the license fee from the Canadian publisher.

Who controls the price
which he will receive for selling his rights under the license system?

I understan5 there is in
the Copyright branch an official who referees in matters of that kind and surely we can leave it to him.
Can my hon. friend say why the estimation of the monetary value of the product of the brain should be left to an officer of a department, whereas one can sell boots and shoes at any price one wants?

That rather begs the question because, if the work is sold in the United States, if the licensing clauses are repealed, the author is done. He does not get anything more than what he gets from the publisher in the United States. If the licensing clauses remain, there is a chance, if his work is of any value, of its being published in Canada and his receiving that additional sum. Whether it is one official or another that decides what the amount is, there will be some amount, and whatever it is, great or small, the author is that much to the good. I do not think it can be maintained that any author has suffered, in the slightest degree, from the operation of this section.
If it is such a good disposition in favour of the printers and others, how many licenses have been asked for during the last two years? The authors certainly would not ask for licenses.

I may point out to my
hon. friend that this licensing section and this act have not been in operation for two years.
Since 1921.
It was passed in 1921 but it was not brought into operation then.

Does my hon. friend
know that not one license has been granted?

I do not. On the contrary I know that some licenses have been granted, certain works have been published and certain publishers have been able to make arrangements to publish those under the licensing sections. At a later stage, I might give my hon. friend the names of the books and stories and of the publishers.
Serials.

Let me point out to the
House that this act with its licensing sections, has been in force only one year. The thing is new to the Canadian publisher. You

Copyright Act Amendment
cannot really expect many or great results from the operation of an act of this kind in one year's time. Therefore I do not think it is fair to say that if there have not been many results, the thing is a failure, and I do not think it can be shown by any person that the author of any work in the Dominion of Canada has suffered in reputation, in pocket, in any way. On the contrary his works are now available for publication in Canada if his United States publisher refuses to come here and do that work. Of course, I have no objection to the bili going to a committee; but, like the hon. member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie), I do not propose to accept the principle of the bill and I will give it such opposition as I can, because if the author suffers nothing, as can be maintained, there are other interests, the interests of workingmen who set the type, who do the binding, the press work, and there are the interests of the publishers of this country which are in a sad enough state, as we all know. Those must be considered as well as the interests of the author.

There are nineteen
amending sections in the bill and I understand the hon. gentleman to take exception to section 5, so that there are eighteen other sections to which he makes no reference. Does he imply that those eighteen sections do not interfere with his rights at all but apply solely to the authors themselves? If that is the case, why throw out the bill?

I am referring to what I think is the most important and serious proposal the hon. member makes. I do not think that the House expects us to deal with the subject exhaustively to-night but I do wish hon. members to know, before the matter goes to the committee, that the bill was passed after serious consideration by a committee of this House, and that in its operation no Canadian author is injuriously affected whereas, on the other hand, many interests, including the works of working men in this country, are assisted in the process. If that can be shown then I submit that this House should hesitate before making the changes which my hon. friend proposes.

With reference to the remarks of my hon. friend (Mr. Hocken), I would remind the House that this bill was passed in 1921 in a spirit of compromise and that it was put into force in 1923, again in a spirit of compromise. It was a very comprehensive measure as it %vas brought into the House by the Hon. Mr. Doherty in 1921, and it was sent to a special

committee of which I happened to be a member myself. We were able to agree on practically every clause except the licensing sections, and we agreed at the time in committee that when the bill should come before the House exception would be taken to these sections. Exception was taken at the time; I voiced it myself, and other members spoke as well, pointing out that they were not in conformity with the Berne convention; and the Minister of Justice of that day agreed that if this allegation could be proved the clauses could be withdrawn later on. He suggested, however, as a matter of compromise-and I insist on that-that we should let the bill pass anyway and be incorporated in the statutes. That is why the bill as it passed in 1921 contained in section 50 the proviso that it would come into effect only on a day to be fixed by proclamation of the Governor in Council. Then there was a change in the government of the country and in 1923 I placed a resolution on the order paper proposing to withdraw the licensing clauses. The then Minister of Trade and Commerce brought down a bill to the very same effect and this obviated the necessity for my resolution. When that bill was discussed in the House exception was taken to it by the hon. member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie) and other hon. gentlemen. Finally the government brought in an amendment to that bill, which was virtually an admission that the licensing clauses as they stood in the 1921 bill were not in accordance with the Berne convention.
That has been remedied.

I am coming to that. I hold in my hand the official document from Berne to that effect. It was contended that if Canada wished to adhere to the convention the terms of the licensing clauses should not apply to other nations, although there was nothing to prevent this country from applying it to its own writers. The effect of the amendment brought down by the then Minister of Trade and Commerce was precisely in the terms I have stated, namely, that these clauses should apply to none but Canadian writers.

And those of the United
States.

Yes. At the time of the third reading of the bill I did make a statement to the effect that that amendment would 10 p.m. certainly not suit the purpose of Canadian writers. We took the stand that as the Copyright Act as a whole was quite comprehensive, as it touched other interests, in the field of phonograph records, for instance, as well as in other directions, we were very

Criminal Code Amendment
anxious to have the bill go through as it was tentatively. For that reason we did not press the objection. I must repeat, however, that we never agreed to the special clauses that are now dealt with in the bill brought down by my hon. friend (Mr. Chevrier), and I take exception to the statement that has been made, that this matter was dealt with by parliament and was practically decided on. That is not the case at all. It was shelved and put aside and we agreed to come to it later on. We did not want to block the bill as a whole and that is why it was adopted in 1921 and again, as amended, in 1923, and put into force in 1924, early in January. We are moving for special amendments of a minor character and we also wish to deal with the licensing clauses. As has been stated, however, the matter is a very complicated one and for that reason we desire to have it thoroughly discussed before a special committee. This,
I think, is a fair statement of the case. I am not prejudiced at all; I may be convinced tomorrow that the sections in question should remain in the act. But I think it would be a good thing to take them up before a special committee, and that is why I propose that the bill be read the second time and be referred to the committee. I shall have the honour to second my hon. friend's motion.

speakeroldname: Hon. A. B. COPP (Secretary of State):
speechtext:
Since the bill was introduced I have read it carefully and I agree with hon. gentlemen as to its complexity; it undoubtedly is both complicated and technical. I do not agree with the view that in allowing the second reading of the bill we are necessarily committing ourselves to its contents; in adopting the motion for second reading we are merely approving the necessity for an amendment. It would be impossible to discuss this measure properly in committee of the Whole and it would seem desirable to refer the matter to one of the standing committees. These committees, however, are rather large and I can see no objection to a special committee being appointed. For myself, however, I want to make it perfectly clear that in accepting the second reading of the bill I do not thereby necessarily accept the measure in detail. It seems to me that the bill is one that should receive very careful consideration.
Motion agreed to and bill read the second time. Mr. Chevrier thereupon moved that the said bill be referred to a special committee with power to send for persons, papers and records, and to hear evidence and report from time to time.

Mr. A. W. NEILL (Comox-Albemi) moved the second reading of Bill No. 3, to amend the Criminal Code*-Printer's Liability.
He said: Mr. Speaker, this bill, which I introduced last year and which did not go beyond its second reading on account of private members day having been absorbed by the government, simply requires that every document or circular printed for publication and distribution shall bear on it the name of the publisher. There is also a provision requiring the printer or publisher to retain for six months a register of those who have employed him to do this printing, in order to afford facility to find out who the author of any particular document of that kind is. The reason for this legislation is as follows: During the war the public came to appreciate more perhaps than ever before the %m!ue of propaganda. And it did not cease with the war; it is a common practice nowadays, by means of anonymous documents, to seek to promulgate propaganda which is not always of a desirable character. False statements, libelous statements, scandalous statements, can be circulated in that way without recourse against the author w*ho remains anonymous. They are also used for the circulation of seditious statements. I have in my hand one of these pamphlets which has been circulated. I shall not weary the House by reading it all, but I shall just quote one or two sentences. It goes on to state that the late war was all the cause of England. It says:
Kaiser Wilhelm's telegram to Kruger, the president of the Transvaal, was the answer of brave Germany to the treacherous English.
Again I find this expression:
Under the circumstances it is very logical to find this English monster, with all his power of wealth and cunning craft, acting against the interests of humanity.
And again:
He will ruin the industries of all the nations for the benefit of tiny England. He will try his best to perpetuate disunion between different peoples. It will be, indeed, a hell on earth.
He winds up with the expression:
I simply speak in the interests of our common human family.
The gentleman who sent me this document writes in part as follows-and I would particularly commend the opening paragraph to my hon. friend the member for George Etienne Cartier (Mr. Jacobs). He says:
Enclosed find a small pamphlet which might come in handy if some of our well-meaning but ill-informed M.P's from the east should again bring forward the matter of giving the supposedly greatly abused and loyal Hindus of British Columbia the right of franchise.
Criminal Code Amendment

Of course I am now dealing with the matter from another aspect. Further on he says:
It would be well within the lines of conservative truth to say that the sentiments of this pamphlet are cherished as gospel fact and concurred in by ninety per cent of the Hindus of British Columbia. I myself, after working with them for eighteen years and after having conversed with many of the smartest men, have invariably found this so. The enclosed pamphlet is receiving wide circulation in Hindu among their own people and also in English among the Asiatics who can speak our language. Read and judge for yourself its effect upon ignorant people.
If precedent is needed for this legislation I can point to the Dominion Elections Act, which makes it a criminal offence and, I think, disqualifies a man for seven years, if he circulates practically any statement about his opponent. If it is considered wise to prevent even the making of a remark about your opponent during an election in the form of a circulated document, it surely cannot be very far wrong to take steps against anonymous utterances against your neighbour in a community.
You will note, Mr. Speaker, that the bill does not prohibit the publication of those statements, because it might be a question whether they were right or wrong; it only affords some clue, so to speak, as to who is the author of them. I might further mention, in the matter of precedent, that the act upon which this is founded has been in force in Britain since 1839 and no fault has been found with it in that regard.
I may say further that subsection 334 of the bill provides ample exemptions to take care of any possible injustice that could occur. You will see that everything ;s provided for that could reasonably require consideration in that connection. I have pleasure in moving the second reading of the bill.

May I ask my hon. friend
before he concludes whether he has received any legal advice as to whether or not this bill is within the competence of this parliament?

It has been suggested to me
that the bill might meet the fate of what is known as the Lemieux Act, on the ground- and I think the argument is somewhat farfetched'-that it would traverse the jurisdiction of the provinces, which has to do entirely with civil rights, and might therefore 'be ultra vires of this parliament. Well, I think that is carrying to an extreme and absurd degree the principle on which the Lemieux Act was thrown out. If we are prepared to accept a decision of that kind we may as well tear up half our statutes, notably the Criminal Code.
I picked up at random a few instances of 
clauses of the Criminal Code which might equally be held to be ultra vires if this one is. Here are some of them: The Criminal Code makes it an offence to disturb divine worship. I think it will be generally agreed that divine worship is a civil right rather than one of Dominion jurisdiction. Again, a breach of contract is made an offence under the Criminal Code. Well surely a breach of contract is a civil right and would therefore be held to be under the jurisdiction of the provinces.	The matter of issuing trading
stamps should, I think, be considered one of civil rights. The sale of a wreck without sufficient title comes within what may be regarded as civil rights. The leaving of a quarry unguarded; writing on or interfering with municipal election documents, interfering with private fishing, or, to come down to such small items as these, interfering with a grape vine or a vegetable-I should suppose that any rights with respect to grapevines or growing vegetables would be under the provincial jurisdiction. There is also a somewhat similar item to what I am discussing now; anyone who prints an advertisement offering a reward for a stolen article and undertakes to ask no questions, is liable to prosecution under the Criminal Code. Well, if the matter dealt with under my bill is a civil right, I presume that one would be also. I could refer to a number of other similar instances, but I have given enough to illustrate the idea that if we are going to accept the suggestion that this bill is only intra vires of the provinces, then we are going to eliminate half the Criminal Code, and many of our statutes would be in the same danger. I would suggest that as the question has not been raised in any authoritative way, it would be well to proceed with the act and it would be upon anyone who suffered from its provisions to raise the questions and take the matter to the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council-which I think is an extremely unlikely thing to happen.

Motion agreed to, bill read the second time, and the House went into committee thereon, Mr. Gordon in the chair.
Bill reported.

Mr. JOS. T. SHAW (West Calgary):	Mr. Speaker, I have been requested on behalf of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) to allow this order to stand. I am glad to accede to that request.

Dominion Elections Act
Mr. WILLIAM IRVINE (East Calgary) moved the second reading of Bill No. 5, an act to amend the Dominion Elections Act.
Explain.

Mr. Speaker, in moving the
second reading of this bill I would like to make it clear that I do not by any means think that if we were to pass this bill we would have a very good Elections Act. I think there are -many other points in it that might well be dealt with, but I am proposing the repeal of these clauses 10 and 11 because they are more discriminatory against organized labour. Large corporations have had for a long time the name -of corrupting political parties by their donations. I do not know whether they have done so or not, but I must confess I feel a little -afraid1 as a member of the Labour party lest the Bankers' Association or the Manufacturers' Association may make large donations to us before the next election and possibly help corrupt the Labour -party by donating too much money. At any rate there is a possibility of that.
Remote.

I agree it is very remote,
but we ought to be very7 careful even against remote dangers. However, I will take the risk and ask that these clauses be removed from the statute book.
The purpose of clause 10 of the Dominion Elections Act evidently was to prevent large corporations from making donations to political parties. If this was not the intention, then it was the excuse for inserting this clause, and the covert purpose would be to prevent farmer and labour organizations from taking political action and from financing their political movements. I assume the original intention was to prevent large corporations from contributing -to party funds. I ask that this clause be repealed because of its impotence to do that for which it was intended. It may, of course, be debatable whether or not a company should be prohibited from contributing to a political party which adopts policies which may be favourable to the interests -of that company, but granting for the moment, for the sake of argument, that it is not advisable that a company should contribute from its funds for -political purposes, I contend th-at it is not practicable to prevent them from so doing by clause 10. The best th-at section 10 could possibly do would be to effect an alteration in the manner in which the companies contribute. The
funds would flow a little -more circuitously, but they would -be none the less bountiful than they were before this clause was inserted in the law. Economic interest is a much more potent factor in political affairs than pious wishes or legal clauses drawn on moral grounds. We cannot make a corporation moral by a legal clause, any more than we can make an individual moral by a legal clause. I affirm -that new ways of contributing have been found, and new ways will be found of evading any such legislation. The letter of this particular section of the law is being praised, and its spirit is being mocked. Not only should this clause be repealed because it does not hinder corporations from contributing, bu-t it should be repealed -because of its influence towaids anarchy. It is much better I think, and I am sure the House will agree with me, to have no law than to have one that people enjoy evading, a law that people actually play with as a game to see how easily they can get -around it. Clause 10 affords such a pleasure to those who might be making large contributions to election -funds. By this clause the pain of contributing would b-e offset to a considerable degree by the amount of pleasant excitement which the donor would receive from dodging the law in giving. It becomes a game to break the law. There w-ere too many of these l-aws before this one came. I am not convinced, Mr. Speaker, that manufacturers or any corporation should be stopped from contributing to political parties; I am convinced that they cannot be stopped by legislation of this kind. I -am also convinced that we should stop trying to stop them from contributing if they want to, and for -that reason I ask that this clause be repealed.	_	_
But there is another reason why this bill should pass and that is that clause 10 of the Dominion Elections Act is much more effective against labour than it is in preventing corporations from contributing to -election funds-the purpose for which it was presumably drawn. Large amounts could now be contributed under clause 10 by individuals for corporations and the penalties of the i-aw be very easily evaded, but this is not so in connection with labour unions. This cannot happen in the case of labour because we have no very wealthy labour men who are prepared to donate five or ten or one hundred thousand dollars to an election fund. Election funds in the case of labour have to be collected in twenty-five or fifty cent pieces from individuals. Consequently, while this section may be very easily got over by those corporations against whom it was drawn, labour cannot avoid it quite so easily. It is
Dominion Elections Act

true, of course, that provisions are made for the incorporation of any association of people for political purposes, and this incorporation would afford them the right under the law to contribute and collect funds. 1 want to point out that the labour organization in Canada are not in a position to avail themselves of this part of the election law. The labour organization is an industrial organization, it is acting under an international constitution, and that international constitution prohibits it from becoming incorporated for political purposes. For this reason the labour organization is unable to do what the organized farmers had to do in order to avoid the penalties of this section. The latter body became incorporated for political purposes and thus fulfilled the demands of the Dominion Elections Act. But labour is not in a position to do that, and consequently this section causes a particular hardship to fall on the labour organization. Now labour people hate to have to dodge the law for the contribution of a quarter or fifty cents as the case might be. If it were $100,000 or so, it might :be worth the trouble, but when it is the case of a small donation, perhaps given by a trade union voluntarily, it is impossible for them to get around this act without a great deal of inconvenience. I contend, therefore, that this section should be repealed in order that a labour organization might voluntarily vote money to the funds of any party-Conservative, Liberal, Progressive or any other party-that they might wish, and that legislation -which stands in the way of this voluntary action is certainly reactionary.
There is another point to which I would like to draw the attention of the House in this regard and it is, that this as one more means which stands in the way of preventing organized labour from seeking to take action in a constitutional manner. Much talk has been uttered in the past about the industrial action which labour men throughout Canada had taken at various times; it has been contended that they should adopt political methods, and that they should take political action and bring their grievances to parliament. But when they begin to take such action as is termed constitutional they find section 10 prohibits them from adopting that method. Perhaps at this point I had better read section 10 in order that there will be no misunderstanding as to what its import is. It reads as follows:
No unincorporated company or association and no incorporated company or association other than one incorporated for political purposes alone shall directly or indirectly, contribute, loan, advance, pay, or promise or offer to pay any money or its equivalent 
to, or for, or in aid of, any candidate at an election, or to, or for, or in aid of, any political party, committee, or association, or to, or for, or in aid of, any company incorporated for political purposes, or to, or for, or in furtherance of, any political purpose whatever, or for the indemnification or reimbursement of any person for money so used.
Every director, shareholder, officer, attorney, or agent of any company or association violating the provisions of this section, or who aids, abets, advises, or takes part in any such violation, and every person who asks or knowingly receives any money or its equivalent in violation of the provisions of this section, is guilty of an indictable offence against this act punishable as in this act provided.
Do I understand that the principal object of the bill is to allow labour organizations to contribute to electoral funds?
Yes, the principal object I am seeking to gain by asking a repeal of this section is that labour may be allowed to contribute to election funds.

May I suggest to my hon. friend that an amendment to the section would serve his purpose, an amendment just putting in two or three words after the following:
No unincorporated company or association and no incorporated company or association other than one incorporated for political purposes-
I suggest the addition there of the words: " or labour organization ", That would serve the purpose of my hon. friend.

I am quite aware that such would have served my purpose, but having discussed this matter with a goodly number of the members of the House I found they would be more willing to repeal this clause than to grant a particular privilege to labour or to any other group of people in the country. I felt also that I did not wish to ask even for a labour organization what I was not prepared to grant to similar organizations throughout Canada. Therefore I came to the conclusion that the best thing to do would be to repeal the whole clause.
I would also d'raw attention to section 11 which this bill also proposes to repeal. Perhaps I had better read that section. It says:
Any person, not being an elector or a candidate, who resides without Canada and who, to secure the election of any candidate, canvasses for votes or in any way endeavours to induce voters to vote for any candidate at an election, or to refrain from voting, is guilty of an indictable offence against this act punishable as in this act provided.
I do not know any case where this has been enforced; I think it would be too absurd to be enforced. We often have labour men from Great Britain who write to our papers at election time. They might possibly be coming to this country during an

Dominion Elections Act
election, and we could' not ask even Ramsay MacDonald, the ex-premier of Great Britain, to take part in an election in Centre Winnipeg, because this particular section would prohibit us. That I say is absurd.
Would it not be the height of bad taste for Mr. Ramsay MacDonald to come in here and assist any person to carry an election?

Possibly it would. It is
not a matter of taste that I am dealing with, it is the matter of the absurdity of this provision in the law. I think we can take it for granted, however, that if taking part in an election involved any flagrant departure from good taste a man of the calibre of the expremier of Great Britain would not take advantage of it. Consequently we do not need to have any precaution against that kind of thing. I want to say to my hon. friend that it is not unknown for Canadians to take part in elections in Great Britain, and there are no provisions in their statutes which prohibit us from doing that. I do not see why we should have such a ridiculous provision as this which might be used against perhaps very eminent men or women from Great Britain. I do not think it is necessary to argue this thing. I repeat that it is absurd. It is not enforced because of its absurdity, and why it should be here as a club over the labour organizations I fail to see. In conclusion let me point out, Mr. Speaker, that in the Election Act of Great Britain provision is made for labour people to contribute to election funds. I would also point out that in the memorandum submitted by representatives of organized labour in Canada to the government this year the repeal of these sections is urged. I hope the House will agree with me that it is in the interests of good law and the interests of Canada as a whole that sections 10 and 11 should be repealed.

The bill which the hon. member for East Calgary (Mr. Irvine) has presented to the House for second reading is one of great importance and very sweeping. Sections 10 and 11 of the Dominion Elections Act of the year 1920 were passed in this House under the guidance of my hon. friend from South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie), who was then Solicitor General, and they were fully debated and carefully considered by the House at that time. Even then there was nothing new in the matter then incorporated into those sections. They both came down from the year 1908 with some slight amendments. In fact I think the first one went back as far as
1898. The provisions made in those sections are really very essential and very necessary The debate held in 1920, when the whole Elections Act was drafted, dealt with the necessity of preventing corporations using their funds in elections. The necessity of that is very apparent. It was a fact that in this country, and in the United States and other countries, large interests and corporations had not hesitated at times to use their funds in election matters, and the following section was passed:
No unincorporated company or association and no incorporated company or association other than one incorporated for political purposes alone shall, directly or indirectly, contribute, loan, advance, pay, or promise or offer to pay any money or its equivalent to, or for, or in aid of, any candidate at an election.
A political association can be formed and moneys can be contributed' by that association, but this went further and said:
Every director, shareholder, officer, attorney, or agent of any company or association violating the provisions of this section, or who aids, abets, advises, or takes part in any such violation, and every person who asks or knowingly receives any money or its equivalent in violation of the provisions of this section, is guilty of an indictable offence against this act punishable as in this act provided.
And the fine for the violation of this section was increased, I think rightly and properly so. The reasoning of this would be very apparent. This is not aimed at labour, as my hon. friend the mover of the bill suggests at all. It is broad and involves all corporations. The necessity is plain. Funds in a corporation, and funds in a labour union are there for specific purposes. What right has a corporation to use funds for election matters when these funds were subscribed for an altogether different purpose? Now section 11 reads:
Any person not being an elector or candidate, who resides without Canada and who, to secure the election of any candidate, canvasses for votes or in any way endeavours to induce voters to vote for any candidate at an election, or to refrain from voting, is guilty of an indictable offence against this act punishable as in this act provided.
The notable point about that section is that it deals with the period during which an election is in operation, and that is defined by clause (d) of the interpretation, which says:
" During an election " or " at an election " or " throughout an election " includes the period after the issue of the writ for an election, or after the dissolution of parliament or the occurrence of a vacancy in consequence of which a writ for an election is eventually issued, until the elected candidate is returned as elected.
That simply prohibits people from outside of Canada, at the very period when an elec-

Dominion Elections Act
tion is going on in this country, a matter of 30 or 40 days, from coming here and canvassing for votes, and taking a part in the election, and the reason for it is very apparent. We have embodied in this act measures to see that elections are conducted properly, and that no irregularities shall occur, and if outsiders were allowed to come to Canada they would be at liberty to conduct elections in a way that people at home here in Canada could not do and readily escape back to their own country. This applies not only to labour, but it is applicable to all classes of people. Wealthy corporations in the United States, with branch offices in Canada, cannot come into this country and canvass and take part in an election or induce the people to vote or to refrain from voting. The hon. gentleman who promotes the bill has laid stress on these two subsections as being calculated tc injure labour. That was not the intention at all. The very language of the clause does not indicate that. It applies to all sections of the community, to all occupations, to every type of citizen at an election time. As another hon. gentleman pointed out, it would be very easy for the mover of the bill to have excepted labour unions or trade unions in this clause. Not content with doing that he actually proposes in this House to sweep out all these safeguards that protect us from fraud, and so on, at an election time, and in that way I say that the bill he has proposed is very vital and very serious.

May I ask the minister if
an exception with respect to labour were incorporated into the existing legislation would he approve of it?

I would say to my
hon. friend-and I intended to mention it in any event-that the government proposes before the close of the session to introduce a bill introducing some amendments to the Elections Act. There have been several reports made by the electoral officers since the Dominion Elections Act was passed. There are some amendments not of a sweeping character that we feel the House would concur in fully, and when sufficient information can be gathered a bill will be brought down in due course, but I would suggest to the mover of the bill that it would be better possibly if he would drop the bill; and consideration might be given to hi? proposal. I cannot urge him to drop it. The government bill will be considered in committee, and he will have a chance in committee when the bill is brought down to discuss the question he has raised in this House. But the House will see that this 
bill as drafted is simply sweeping away what has been on our statute books for a long time and exists there of apparent necessity. The government could not consent to the passing of the second reading of this bill at the present time.
Since this legislation has been on the statute books for so long, can the minister say that he thinks it has been effective?

I think there is no doubt of that at all. I cannot tell what corporations might have done if the act had not been passed. We find it necessary to pass many laws against crimes of all kinds and generally they are effective, and I presume this law has been effective in this case. Surely the hon. member would not propose to throw down all the safeguards that we have.
Does the minister find any objections to provision being made by which labour organizations could provide funds for political purposes, such as is proposed in principle by the mover?
That is a matter for the deliberate consideration of the House. No man in this country is more friendly to labour than I am.
Answer the question.

There would be great difficulties in that. Supposing my hon. friend was a member of a trade union and he put his money in it for the purposes of trade union work. Would he want the directors or officers of that union to vote it away for an entirely different purpose?
Would the members of the union not decide that for themselves?

That is where the
difficulty arises.

The matter contained in this bill may be viewed from two different angles. I can say frankly that when this measure was introduced in 1920, I think it was, political movement was pretty lively out on the prairies and the farmers were taking a stand to go into politics actively. There was some suspicion at that time that this law was aimed at movements of this character. Since then I have viewed the matter very carefully and we found a way of getting around it in a perfectly legal manner by becoming incorporated for political purposes. That may seem, on the face of it, to be a rather cumbersome way of carrying on political activities Thinking the matter over, I have now come

Dominion Elections Act
to the conclusion that, perhaps, it is just as well to avoid the very appearance of evil, and if people wish to go into politics actively in a body, I do not think there is any great hardship in asking that they should become incorporated if they wish to collect funds for that purpose. I quite sympathize with the ideas of the promoter of this bill in that he may think it a hardship that they should be compelled to incorporate for this purpose. Nevertheless, I am inclined to believe that the law as it stands now may have a very good effect as a warning to corporations and bodies of individuals who may wish to contribute towards political funds for the purpose of corrupting the public. In fact, I would be inclined to allow the law as it stands in section 10 to remain as it is.
As regards section 11, I am not so sure. I cannot, however, see that a great deal of harm would occur in allowing outsiders to come in and take part in our elections. As has already been said, Canadians go over to Great Britain, take part in the elections over there and get elected as members of the Imperial parliament. It is, perhaps, an open question just how far that should be allowed. I have listened to remarks made by the Solicitor General as regards foreigners coming in here, acting in a corrupt manner and then leaving abruptly so that they cannot be punished for what they have done. That may be perfectly true, but at the same time I would allow liberty of action in a matter of this kind and I would be inclined to be in favour of section 11 being withdrawn.
Hon. GEORGE P. GRAHAM (Minister of Railways and Canals): Mr. Speaker, I have to admit that I have been in public life in Canada longer than the hon. member for East Calgary (Mr. Irvine), and I will give him the reasons why this section prohibiting outsiders from taking part in our elections was placed in the statute book in the first place. As a matter of fact, it was to prevent any party from bringing men, lately from across the border, to take part in our elections. Many years ago, when this act was first passed, each party was charging the other with importing men trained in election manipulation from various cities in the United States to assist them in doing in the campaign in Canada, work which the Canadian under the law would not dare to do himself. That was the basis of this law. My hon. friend will say, of course, that if a man was caught plugging, he could be arrested, but the difficulty was that he would do that kind of work, every person would know that he was in the country doing political work for
some of the parties, but they could not discover until election day, perhaps, a direct violation of our law. Under the statute as it stands now, he could be arrested if he was found taking part in an election and you would not have to prove a direct violation of our election law in order to arrest him. If my hon. friend had passed through the experiences, particularly in the border counties, that many of us in Canada did years ago, he would not think of removing this restriction. There has been a great improvement in election methods since it became a part of our statutes. It never was intended to apply to a man like Ramsay MacDonald or any other man who, passing through the country, wished1 to make a speech, and a law is only justifiable in the way it is enforced. A law must be enforced With common sense or it will not remain law very long. I might warn my hon. friend that if he would persist in removing that section, we might have a return to the days when we were infested at election time with men brought across the border to do certain work that Canadians would not do themselves.

In connection with tire time at which the first section was adopted, my recollection is that it was adopted in 1920, and I was rather surprised to hear the Solicitor General state that it dates back to 1908. Perhaps he or the hon. member lor South Wellington can give some authoritative information on that point.

The present Dominion Elections Act was drafted' in 1920. This particular section 10 comes, I think, from the Elections Act of 1908, with a slight amendment dealing with the opening words, "an unincorporated company or association," and the penalty was increased. Section 10 is substantially as it stood in the prior act. There is nothing new in the enactment in the statute of 1920. Section 11 is also the same.

If my recollection serves me, clause 10 dates further back than the Elections Act of 1907. it was passed in 1898 and has been carried now on the statutes for over a quarter of a century. The other clause was passed in the year 1907 or 1908. My own opinion is that in view of the suggestion of the Solicitor General (Mr. McMurray), the hon. member who has moved this bill (Mr. Irvine) would do well to drop the matter pending the bringing down later on of the bill which the government proposes to introduce during the session. I assume that there will be quite a number of amendments to be pro-
Motions

posed to the Dominion Elections Act. Some the Solicitor General says are of minor importance while others may be of greater significance. But there will be an opportunity then for the hon. member to move an amendment in the ordinary course as in the case of any other public bill. I think he would be well advised in the meantime to let this bill drop with the idea of reviving it, if he sees fit, when the general bill is under discussion. In the meantime we could give the matter further consideration.
Motion (Mr. Irvine) negatived.

On the motion of Mr. Church:
For a copy of all papers, agreements, correspondence, telegrams and letters exchanged between the government of Canada, the governments of Ontario and the United States, and the Hydro-Electric Commission regarding the generation and distribution of power at what is commonly known as the proposed Morrisburg dam on the St. Lawrence river.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The wording of this motion contemplates something more than it is possible for the government to comply with. It calls for all correspondence and so on exchanged between the government of Canada, the governments of Ontario and the United States and the Hydro-Electric Commission. We clearly are not in a position to bring down papers exchanged between the government of Ontario and the Hydro-Electric Commission, or between the United States and the commission. In other words, we can bring down only such papers as have passed between the government of Canada and any of the bodies mentioned in the motion that is to say, any correspondence to which this government has been
11 p.m. a party. If the hon. member will amend his motion to carry that meaning it may pass. I suggest that he insert after the words " the government of Canada " the word " and," and substitute the word " or " for the word " and " before the words " the Hydro-Electric Commission." If the motion is amended in that way it may be adopted.
Motion as amended agreed to.

On the motion of Mr. Church:
For a copy of all papers, agreements, correspondence, letters and other data exchanged between the government of Canada and the governments of the municipalities or provinces, relating to unemployment, including a return as to what action was taken at conferences between the aforesaid governments on this question, and showing the amount spent on unemployment by the government of Canada during the past four years for unemployment relief.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I do not like to be critical, but my hon. friend uses an expression which is hardly appropriate-" the governments of the municipalities or provinces". I would suggest that he drop the words " governments of the ".
Motion as amended agreed! to.

On the motion of Mr. Church:
For returns showing-1. The amount spent by the government of Canada in relieving unemployment in Canada in Winnipeg, Hamilton, Toronto, Vancouver and Montreal during the past six years.
2.	What sum respectively was spent by the (a) Dominion government, (b) the provincial government, (c) the municipalities aforesaid, relieving unemployment in these five cities the past six years.
3.	Whether the government during these years had any agreement with the provinces and municipalities as to any form of relief; if so, what the arrangement was.
4.	Whether any steps have been taken during this winter by the government alone or with the provinces or municipalities to take care of unemployment, and to regulate and prevent the dumping of those out of work in the larger centres of population.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
My hon. friend has a genius for asking for material to which he is not entitled. Section 2 of this motion asks for information regarding moneys spent by the Dominion government, certain provincial governments and certain municipalities. This government has no information and is not in a position to supply any in regard to what was spent either by the provincial governments or by the municipalities; and the rest of the second paragraph is therefore only a repetition of the first. If the hon member will delete the second! clause altogether the government will be prepared to comply with the remainder of the motion. I suggest, therefore, that the motion be amended accordingly.
Motion as amended agreed to.
